articles.title: Building an Open-Source Support Tool That Turns Your Docs into Reusable Knowledge
articles.description: I spend a good part of my day working with the community at CopilotKit, answering questions in...
articles.body_html:
I spend a good part of my day working with the community at CopilotKit, answering questions in Discord, GitHub, and Slack, helping people get unstuck, and pointing them to the right resources.

I started building answerLoops to help me with that work. As it took shape, I added integrations for more platforms so other teams could use it in their communities too.

It’s open source, and I’m building it in public.

Explore answerLoops on ⭐️ GitHub

A big part of the work has been deciding how knowledge gets into the system. Some answers are in the docs. Others come out of a support conversation or are things someone on the team just knows.

For an agent to use those answers, the team needs a straightforward way to save them, review them, and keep them current. That’s what I’ve been building into the knowledge base.

Answering the question is only part of the work

A question comes in. You find the relevant documentation or resource, figure out how it applies to that person’s setup, and write a reply.

During that conversation, you might discover something the docs don’t cover. A missing setup step, a confusing default, or a workaround that deserves its own article.

You resolve the question, but that useful detail stays buried in the conversation. When someone else asks, the team has to find it again.

I want answerLoops to help with both parts: preparing a useful answer now and saving what the team learns for future questions.

What answerLoops does

answerLoops is an open-source AI support tool that brings questions from Discord, Slack, GitHub, Telegram, and other connected channels into one dashboard. It uses your knowledge base to help prepare answers.

For knowledge-based replies in the ticket pipeline, a Mastra agent generates a draft and a separate agent scores its confidence and whether it fully answers the question. Automatic replies are off by default. When enabled, answers that meet the configured criteria can be sent automatically; other drafts remain available for human review.

There’s also an embeddable website chat widget built with CopilotKit and connected to a Mastra support agent. Visitors can ask questions directly, with published knowledge-base articles supplied as reference material.

The widget supports richer responses, including step-by-step guides, quick replies, callouts, link cards, and contact options.

But the quality of those answers depends on the information available to the agent. That’s why much of the recent work has been on the knowledge base.

Add the answer that isn’t in your docs

Sometimes you don’t need to import a documentation site. You just need to write down something the agent should know.

An owner or admin can open Knowledge Base → Manage and use Write an answer by hand:

  1. Enter a question or title.
  2. Write the answer or context.
  3. Click Add to knowledge base.

For example, a customer might ask whether changing a configuration requires a restart. Someone on your team knows the answer, but it isn’t documented anywhere.

The article is published and indexed when it’s saved, making it available for subsequent questions. There’s no draft step in this form, so the answer should be suitable for customers to read.

Adding an article doesn’t retrain the model. It gives the agent another reference to retrieve when a relevant question comes in.

Articles added this way appear under Added by hand in the Knowledge coverage tab.

It’s a small feature, but it gives the person with the answer a direct way to improve what the agent knows.

Bring in the knowledge you already have

You can also populate the knowledge base from existing content:

  • Documentation URLs: import a page or crawl a documentation site.
  • Files: upload PDF, DOCX, Markdown, text, or CSV files.
  • GitHub: sync Markdown and MDX files, with optional syncs when changes are pushed to the default branch.
  • Notion: connect pages and databases your team wants to use.

Notion content imports unpublished. Your team can inspect it before making it available for customer-facing answers, and that publishing choice is preserved across syncs.

The manual-entry form sits alongside these sources. If an answer already exists in your docs, import it. If it only exists in someone’s head, write it down.

Turn a resolved ticket into reusable knowledge

Closing a ticket helps the person who asked. Turning that resolution into a knowledge-base article makes the explanation available for future questions.

The Promote to KB action lets an owner or admin turn that ticket’s question and answer into a knowledge-base article.

Before promoting it, check that the answer applies beyond the original conversation. Remove account-specific details and make the explanation useful to someone encountering the same problem later.

This matters for the website widget in particular. Its retrieved reference material comes from published KB articles, rather than raw resolved tickets.

Promoting an answer gives it a place in the shared knowledge base where the widget can find it.

Let customer questions help you decide what to write

You won’t know every gap in your documentation ahead of time.

The Review tab captures questions that weren’t covered by the available knowledge. On hosted plans, this queue is available on Pro and above.

A usable draft can come along as a starting point. If there isn’t one, the item is marked No usable answer, and someone can write it.

Owners and admins can edit the question and answer, then choose Approve and add to knowledge base. If the item shouldn’t become an article, they can reject it instead.

Nothing in the queue becomes searchable customer-facing knowledge until it’s approved.

When the same question comes in again, its counter increases instead of creating another copy. The most-asked questions appear first.

If several people ask about the same setup step, that’s a useful signal about what your knowledge base is missing. The queue gives your team a question to work from and a place to review the answer before publishing it.

Go from a knowledge gap to a new article

The Knowledge Gaps page provides another view of where support needs attention.

It surfaces tickets with low-confidence answers, tickets that need a person, and resolved questions without a covering KB article.

Repeated questions are grouped with an Asked N times badge, so you can see recurring topics without reading every ticket separately.

The + KB action opens the manual-entry form with the ticket’s question and any existing answer filled in. Review the text, add the article, and it’s linked back to the ticket to close that gap.

You don’t have to leave the question behind and start a blank document somewhere else.

Check what the agent can actually find

Importing a document doesn’t tell you whether it will help with a particular question.

The Knowledge coverage tab shows articles grouped by source, including whether they’re live, unpublished, or not searchable.

There’s also a Try a customer question field. It runs the same lookup the website widget uses and shows which articles match—or that nothing covers the question.

After adding an answer, try the original customer question and a few variations. Does the lookup find the article you just wrote? If it doesn’t, you have something concrete to investigate before judging the generated reply.

This checks retrieval, not whether every generated reply will be correct. You still need to review the answers themselves. But it gives you a way to investigate whether the intended information is being found.

The KB is the source of product knowledge your team maintains for the agent. If no article matches, the assistant can fall back to general knowledge, which may not fit your product. Finding those gaps and adding the right material is part of maintaining it.

See which articles are being used

answerLoops also tracks article usage.

It counts when an article is supplied as context for an answer that is actually produced, including website replies and ticket drafts.

The distinction matters: this means the article was given to the agent, not necessarily that the final reply quoted it.

Searches and simulations don’t increase the count.

Together with the coverage view and repeated-question counts, this helps you understand what information is being retrieved and where more work might be useful.

Where CopilotKit and Mastra fit

I work in DevRel at CopilotKit, so part of building answerLoops is putting the tools I work with into a product and sharing what I learn.

Mastra runs the agents behind the support drafts and website conversation, including the chat agent’s thread memory.

CopilotKit provides the foundation for the custom widget interface. The application connects that interface to the agent and supplies the relevant knowledge-base context.

The product also has its own workflows around those pieces: importing sources, reviewing unanswered questions, publishing articles, and handling staff actions on tickets.

Those workflows are where the team gets to improve the information the agent uses. Someone can spot a missing answer, write it, publish it, and check whether a future question retrieves it.

That’s become a much bigger part of answerLoops as I’ve kept building.

Try it and tell me what’s missing

I started this to help with my own community work. I’m sharing it so other developers and support teams can try it in theirs.

The code and setup instructions are on GitHub. You can explore how retrieval, the review queue, and the integrations work, or run answerLoops yourself. The knowledge-base documentation walks through the workflows in this article.

If it looks useful, give the repo a ⭐️. If you try it, tell me what worked and what got in your way.

New to contributing to open source? Reach out—I’d be happy to help you find a place to start.

Where does your team keep the useful answers that haven’t made it into the docs yet?

articles.title: 2 Agent Skills Every Frontend Developer Should Try
articles.description: I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I...
articles.body_html:
I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I found two new ones I want to share with you.

First one is Impeccable. Impeccable took a plain, AI-built website and gave it a design. It wasn't bad at all! Diagram Design took that same site and drew a diagram of how it works! Both install with one command, and both work with basically any coding harness. I used Kiro in my demos but you can use whatever you like.

I made a video walking through both if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • An agent that supports Agent Skills. I use Kiro, but Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex work too.
  • Node.js, so you can run npx.
  • A frontend project to try them on. Mine is a small website about cats.

Finding skills

I found both skills on Skill Leaderboard, which ranks skill repos by GitHub stars. You can filter by compatible agent, so I set it to Kiro. Skills are like recipes that work across most coding harnesses, so you'll usually be fine without the filter. Some repos are easier to install in one agent than another, though, and the filter saves you from finding that out the hard way.

Stars measure popularity. I cared more about what fits my own projects, so I picked the two that match what I build most, which is websites.

Before you install anything, read the SKILL.md and any scripts it pulls in. A skill is instructions and scripts that run with your agent's permissions, so check it the same way you'd check an npm package.

1. Impeccable

Impeccable is a design skill that started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill and builds on top of it. It has UX planning, a set of design commands like critique, polish, and audit, and it asks you a lot of questions.

To test it, I had Claude Opus 5.5 vibe code a site called the Great Cat Color Census. You spot a cat in the wild, click "Spotted one," and the counts and leaderboard update. Out of the box it came with a blocky card style and some hover animations. It looked okay. I don't think it looked bad, but it was pretty generic.


The default design Claude Opus 5.5 came up with.

Install it from your project root:

npx impeccable install

Then run init inside your agent:

/impeccable init

Init looks through the project, asks about anything it can't work out on its own, and writes a PRODUCT.md with what it learned. After that I asked it to make the site much nicer using its styles. It came back with five or six design directions. I picked the sticker one.


The sticker direction from Impeccable. Same features, new design.

It has basically the same features as before, and you can still summon a random cat. It looks a lot more polished, with extra animation and cats that look like peel-off stickers. The font gives it a Cat in the Hat feel. I don't have a very particular taste for frontend design, and I still like this version better. If you're a designer, tell me in the comments whether you agree.

A good way to use Impeccable is to have it build several of its directions on separate Git branches. Then you can run each one and compare them side by side before you commit to a look.

2. Diagram Design

Diagram Design draws diagrams as one self-contained HTML and SVG file. It supports 45 diagram types, from architecture diagrams and flow charts to radar charts and Venn diagrams. The screenshots in the repo don't do it much justice.

Install it with the skills CLI:

npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design

I asked it for a diagram of the same cat site and didn't say what to diagram. There's no backend, so I wasn't expecting much. It picked the visitor flow. A visitor clicks, an action runs change() or reset(), the counts update, and the derived stats feed the left and right pages. It also shows the save and load path to localStorage, and it even carried over the pink styling from the site.


The diagram Diagram Design made from the cat site, open in Kiro.

It's a simple diagram, but I like the style, and I can see myself using it on my next project. It's also handy when you open a code base with little documentation. Ask it for a few diagrams before you start reading the code.

The rest of the list

I haven't spent much time with the other popular skills yet. These are my notes so far.

Ponytail gives your agent the personality of the laziest senior dev in the room. In its README, you show him fifty lines, and he says nothing and replaces them with one. The goal is less code and fewer tokens. In Kiro it loads as an always-on ruleset, so you don't get its slash commands.

Caveman makes the agent answer tersely to cut token usage. I haven't seen much savings myself. Someone in a Reddit thread on the top Kiro skill repos said it raised their token usage, even though the research the repo cites says otherwise.

Addy Osmani's agent skills add a spec, plan, build, and test workflow to your agent. Kiro has specs built in, but if your tool doesn't, this or Superpowers is how I'd add spec-driven development.

I haven't tried UI UX Pro Max or Graphify yet, even though they're near the top of the list.

If you build on AWS, look at the Agent Toolkit for AWS. It's our set of skills and MCP servers for working with AWS from your agent, and it's free on GitHub.

Wrap up

If you build websites, Impeccable is the one I'd install first. Diagram Design is right behind it, especially when you're new to a code base.

I'm thinking about testing whether Ponytail and Caveman save tokens in Kiro. Leave a comment if you want to see that, and tell me which skills you're using.

articles.title: How I landed a dev job with no degree
articles.description: I don't have a computer science degree. I have a job writing software, and I've had one for a while...
articles.body_html:
I don't have a computer science degree. I have a job writing software, and I've had one for a while now. For about a year before that, I did almost everything you're "supposed" to do to make up for the missing degree — and I want to tell you that it worked, because then this would be a nicer story. It didn't. The things I did to compensate for not having a degree were a dead end, and the thing that actually got me hired had nothing to do with the degree at all.

Here's the part that took me far too long to understand: a degree is not the thing employers want. It's a stand-in for the thing they want. And I spent months building a worse stand-in instead of just handing them the real thing.

What I thought "no degree" meant (and what it actually meant)

When you don't have the degree, the whole world tells you the same thing: you have a gap, so go fill it. So I did. I collected certificates — the free ones, then the ones with a logo people recognize. I started a LeetCode streak because a forum told me that's how you prove you're "rigorous" like the CS grads. I enrolled in enough of a bootcamp to get a bootcamp line on my résumé.

Every one of those was me trying to build a replacement credential. A thing I could point at and say: see, I'm as legitimate as the degree. I was playing the degree's game, just with cheaper pieces.

And it got me nothing. Not one interview traced back to a certificate. Not one interviewer asked about my LeetCode. The bootcamp line never came up in a room where someone decided whether to hire me. I had spent months manufacturing proof of the wrong thing.

The rule: when you don't have the credential, the instinct is to build a substitute credential. That's the trap. A certificate is a weaker copy of a degree, and nobody was ever going to want your weaker copy of the thing they already don't fully trust.

The question the degree is actually answering

Here's the reframe that changed everything, and it's the whole article, so I'll say it plainly.

When an employer sees a CS degree on a résumé, they are not thinking "ah, four years of theory." They're a human being trying to de-risk a hire, and the degree answers exactly one question for them:

"Will this person take something hard and ambiguous, with no syllabus and no answer key, and actually finish it?"

That's it. That's what the degree buys. Four years of someone being handed vague, difficult problems and grinding them to completion whether they felt like it or not. The employer doesn't care about the compiler-theory exam. They care that you've got a track record of finishing ambiguous hard things, because that's the entire job, and hiring someone who can't do that is expensive.

The degree is a proxy for finish-ability. A decent one — which is why it works as a filter. But it's a proxy. And once I saw that, the move was obvious and it was not "get a better proxy."

The rule: you cannot out-credential a degree. You will always lose that fight. So don't have it. Skip the proxy entirely and hand them the thing the proxy only gestures at — direct, checkable evidence that you finish hard things nobody scoped for you.

A certificate is also a proxy for finish-ability — a much weaker one, because everyone knows a course is scoped so you can't fail. That's precisely why it carries no weight. I'd been trying to beat a strong proxy with a weak proxy. The answer was to stop competing on proxies and show up with the real signal.

What the real signal looks like

The real signal is embarrassingly simple to describe and genuinely hard to fake: something you built that a stranger uses and that broke on you and that you kept running anyway.

That sentence has three load-bearing parts, and a tutorial project has none of them:

  • A stranger uses it. Not you, not the instructor's spec — a person who does things you didn't plan for. A course project can't have this; the scope is fixed so you always win.
  • It broke. Real usage produces real failure. The todo app from a tutorial never breaks, because nobody's hammering it at 9pm on a Saturday with input you didn't imagine.
  • You kept it running. This is the finish. Not "I built it," which is the fun part, but "it fell over and I was the one who had to get up and fix it with no next-lesson button." That is the exact thing the degree was vouching for.

When you have that, the degree question doesn't just get answered — it stops being asked. Which brings me to the room.

The moment it actually stopped mattering

I'll give you the specific interview, because it's where the abstract thing became real.

Interviewer looks at my résumé, no degree line, and asks the question you're dreading — some polite version of "so, no formal background?" The old me would have gone into defense: listed the certs, mentioned the bootcamp, talked about how much I'd studied. Defending the weak proxy. It reads as exactly what it is — an apology.

Instead I said: "Right — let me tell you about the booking tool I built for a small business. It double-booked two real customers on a Saturday because of a race condition in my code, the owner called me, and I found it and fixed it that morning before they reopened." And I watched the question evaporate. We spent the next twenty minutes on the race condition. Nobody came back to the degree, because I'd just answered the only thing the degree was ever a proxy for, with a story that was checkable and specifically mine.

The rule: you don't win the "no degree" conversation by defending the gap. You make the gap irrelevant by answering — before they can even finish asking — the one question the degree was standing in for. A real war story closes that door in a sentence. A certificate reopens it.

The difference between "I studied this" and "this happened to me and I handled it" is the difference between a proxy and the real thing. One of them is a vibe. The other is checkable, and in the room, checkable wins.

The uncomfortable part: how I shipped enough real things in time

Here's the bit that stings, and I'd rather say it straight. You cannot produce that signal from reading. The signal only exists on the other side of shipped and used, and you need more than one, and you don't have four years. There's a brutal chicken-and-egg here: the evidence that gets you the job can only be made by doing the job, and nobody's employing you to do it yet.

The only way I got through it was to stop treating "build the app" and "understand the app" as the same task. I'd get something live as fast as I possibly could — real database, real URL, a real person able to hit it — and then go back and read it, break it on purpose, and rebuild the parts I didn't understand. Backwards from how courses teach it. It's also the only order that produces a real user, because a thing that's live is a thing that can break on you, and a thing that breaks on you is the only thing that generates a war story.

The rule: a deployed app with one real user teaches you more in a week than a tutorial does in a month — because the user does the thing you swore nobody would do, and now it's your problem with no answer key. That problem is the curriculum, and it hands you the exact fundamentals you need in the exact order you need them.

I learned more real fundamentals debugging that live booking race than in every course combined. The point was never "don't learn." The point is that the live app was the learning, and it also happened to be the evidence. One activity, both outputs.

If you're where I was

You don't need my exact path and you definitely don't need my mistakes. Stop manufacturing proof of the wrong thing and start manufacturing the right one:

  • Quit collecting proxies. One more certificate will not move the needle. You are not trying to look as legitimate as a grad; you're trying to make legitimacy irrelevant.
  • Pick something one real person actually needs. Not a clone. Your cousin's bookings, your own invoices, the spreadsheet your team is drowning in. Small and real beats big and fake, every time.
  • Ship it before it's good. A live URL with one user beats a flawless repo with none. Deploy embarrassingly early — the point is to get it into the hands that will break it.
  • Then go understand what you shipped. Break it on purpose. Read your own code like a stranger wrote it. That's where fundamentals finally stick and where the war stories come from.
  • Keep the war stories. Every "it broke and I fixed it" is a sentence that answers the degree question and out-performs your entire skills list in the room.

The degree gets people past some automated filters, and I won't pretend it doesn't — I got rejected by plenty of them. But filters aren't where you get hired. You get hired in the room, by a human de-risking a decision, and in that room the only thing that moves is evidence you can take something ambiguous, make it real, and keep it running when it breaks.

The rule: the fastest way to look like a senior while you're still a junior — and the fastest way to make "no degree" a non-event — is to have already shipped something that survived contact with a real user. You can't fake that. And you don't need a degree to have it.

articles.title: I broke an Elementor site on purpose, then built a tool to find the bugs
articles.description: BeeLadybug 0.5 adds CSS hunt: a zero-dependency overlay that tells you WHY a WordPress page looks broken — !important rules, overflow causes, invisible text, click blockers and stretched images.
articles.body_html:
The night I broke my own site

I'm 53, I work in a factory, and in the evenings I build things in vanilla JavaScript.

Lately I've been looking at freelance WordPress jobs. Almost every one of them says the same thing: "Elementor site, layout is broken, fix it."

So I did something a bit crazy. I took an empty test site, installed Elementor, and asked an AI to break it for me — 5 hidden CSS bugs, packed into an encoded script so I couldn't just read the answer.

Then I tried to find them.

It was humbling. The page looked wrong, but the console said nothing. Of course: CSS doesn't throw errors. A bad rule is still a valid rule, so the browser applies it silently. That's exactly why clients say "everything moved and I don't know why."

I found the first bug the slow way — DevTools, Styles panel, unchecking rules one by one until I saw it:

.elementor-section, .e-con { margin-right: -60px !important; }

Twenty minutes for one line. I thought: there must be a faster way.

So I built one: CSS hunt

🐞 BeeLadybug is my zero-dependency debugging overlay. You paste one line in the console and it attaches to any page — WordPress dashboards, Elementor pages, mobile viewports. It already showed element size, classes, display type, FPS and memory.

Version 0.5 adds a new mode: CSS hunt (press F6).

When you hover an element, it tells you what's wrong with it:

  • !important rules that match the element, and where they come from (<style> inline or the stylesheet URL)
  • Overflow causes: which element actually leaves the viewport, plus negative margins
  • Invisible text: color: transparent, opacity: 0, or text the same color as its background
  • Click blockers: what sits on top of the element's center, including fixed ::before / ::after on html / body
  • Stretched images: natural ratio vs rendered ratio, when object-fit is fill

Press S to scan the whole page. Click a line and the element gets a red outline.

The hard part: telling the truth without noise

My first version was technically right and practically useless.

One card overflowing the screen produced ten red lines: the card, its article, its p, its h2… All "overflowing", because they inherited it. A fixed overlay blocking clicks? One warning per element underneath it.

A real developer doesn't want ten alarms. They want the culprit.

So the scan now:

  1. Reports the cause, not the containers. An ancestor is skipped if a descendant overflows by the same amount (±2px).
  2. Groups by cause. Instead of 12 lines you get: 
▾ body::after blocks clicks on 12 elements
    div.elementor-element-629ef32
    img#1301
    summary.elementor-element-3925463
    …
  1. Separates bugs from info. Red = bug. Grey = info, like unreadable sheet: fonts.googleapis.com (cross-origin stylesheets can't be read — that's a browser rule, not a problem on the page).
  2. Keeps the log calm. Hover and DOM-mutation lines are hidden unless you turn on verbose mode (F3). Each issue is logged once per element every 5 seconds. Press P to pin the panel on an element and read it in peace.

The real test

The demo page bugs are easy — I wrote them. The real test was the broken Elementor page, with Elementor V4 "atomic" widgets, Google Fonts, Altervista ad scripts and all the usual mess.

Result: CSS hunt found the click blocker, the negative margin overflow, the invisible button text and the stretched image on a live page I didn't build the bugs for.

Try it

Open any page, press F12, paste this in the console:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.5.3/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Then press F6, hover, and press S.

No build step, no framework, no dependencies. Just vanilla JavaScript.

What I learned

  • CSS bugs are silent. The console won't help you. You need to look at computed styles and geometry.
  • The right answer is not enough. A debugging tool must point to the cause, or it's just another wall of text.
  • Breaking things on purpose is the best teacher. I recommend it to anyone who wants to do WordPress fixes for clients.

I'm still learning. If you try CSS hunt on a broken page and it misses something, tell me in the comments — that's how the next version gets better.

🐞 npm: bee-ladybug

articles.title: 5 Best LLM Gateways
articles.description: As AI applications move from prototypes into production, managing model access becomes a different...
articles.body_html:
As AI applications move from prototypes into production, managing model access becomes a different kind of engineering problem.

At first, connecting an application to OpenAI or Anthropic is relatively straightforward. But as a project grows, teams may need to support multiple providers, control token spending, handle rate limits, recover from provider outages, and monitor how models are being used across different applications.

Building all of that independently can create unnecessary complexity.

This is where an LLM gateway becomes useful. It provides a central layer between applications and model providers, helping teams manage AI traffic without implementing the same infrastructure separately in every project.

I've been looking at how different gateways approach this problem, and one thing stands out: not every gateway is designed for the same environment. Some focus on model access and routing, while others emphasize enterprise governance, API management, or operational visibility.

In this article, I'll compare five LLM gateways worth considering in 2026: Bifrost, LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway, and OpenRouter.

TL;DR

  • Bifrost: A strong option for enterprises that need low-overhead model routing, centralized governance, and integrated MCP capabilities. It also offers virtual keys and other controls for managing AI usage.
  • LiteLLM: A flexible, open-source option for accessing multiple LLM providers through a common interface, with proxy and cost-management features.
  • Kong AI Gateway: Best suited to organizations that want to extend existing API infrastructure and governance practices to AI workloads.
  • Cloudflare AI Gateway: A practical choice for teams looking for AI traffic analytics, caching, rate limiting, and retries within the Cloudflare ecosystem.
  • OpenRouter: Useful for developers who want a straightforward way to access models from different providers through a unified API.

The right choice depends on whether you prioritize enterprise controls, model flexibility, existing infrastructure, or a managed way to access a broad model catalog.

What Is an LLM Gateway?

An LLM gateway is an intermediary layer between an application and one or more large language model providers. Instead of having every application manage provider-specific endpoints, credentials, routing logic, and usage tracking independently, teams can centralize these responsibilities.

For example, an application might send requests to a gateway rather than directly to a model provider. The gateway then routes the request to the configured model, applies relevant policies, and returns the response.

Depending on the platform, this layer may also handle:

  • Model routing and fallback: Direct requests to suitable providers and recover from certain failures.
  • Cost management: Track usage, set budgets, and attribute spending to teams or applications.
  • Authentication and governance: Manage credentials, access permissions, and rate limits.
  • Observability: Monitor requests, token consumption, latency, and errors.
  • Caching: Reuse eligible responses to reduce repeated model calls and costs.
  • MCP and agent integrations: Manage access to tools and services used by AI agents, where supported.

These capabilities can simplify production operations, but the depth of implementation varies considerably between gateways.

How to Evaluate an LLM Gateway

Before comparing individual products, I would look at five practical considerations.

Evaluation criterion What to look for Why it matters
Provider support Compatibility with the models and APIs you use Reduces integration work and provider lock-in
Routing and reliability Fallbacks, load balancing, and provider selection Helps applications handle failures and changing workloads
Governance Authentication, budgets, permissions, and rate limits Makes AI usage easier to control across teams
Observability Request logs, latency, errors, and cost reporting Helps teams troubleshoot and optimize production systems
Deployment Managed, self-hosted, or hybrid options Determines how well the gateway fits security and infrastructure requirements

Performance also deserves attention, particularly when an application makes multiple sequential model calls. Published latency numbers are only useful when the benchmark methodology, hardware, workload, and request volume are understood.

1. Bifrost: Enterprise AI Routing and Governance

Bifrost is an AI gateway developed by Maxim AI that focuses on routing, governing, and observing AI traffic across multiple providers. It offers an OpenAI-compatible interface, allowing teams to integrate supported models without building a separate connection for each provider.

Its architecture is particularly relevant for teams that need an operational control layer rather than just a convenient way to switch models.

What stands out

Bifrost combines several capabilities in one platform:

  • Multi-provider routing: Access supported providers through a common gateway and configure routing or fallback behavior.
  • Performance focus: Bifrost is written in Go, and its maintainers publish benchmarks reporting low gateway overhead under specified test conditions. Teams can review the Bifrost benchmarking documentation to understand the testing approach.
  • Enterprise governance: Virtual keys, access profiles, budgets, and rate limits help teams manage usage across consumers and applications. Its budget and limits controls provide additional options for managing spending and request volume.
  • MCP integration: Its MCP gateway capabilities extend management beyond model requests to interactions with external tools.
  • Operational visibility: Request logs, analytics, and administrative controls help teams understand how AI infrastructure is being used.

The combination is useful when a company wants model routing and governance in the same infrastructure layer. For organizations running AI agents, the ability to manage model requests and MCP tool access can also reduce the need to operate disconnected control systems.

Bifrost is open source, and its GitHub repository provides implementation details for teams evaluating the architecture or considering self-hosted deployment.

Deployment requirements are another consideration. Organizations with specific network restrictions can investigate in-VPC deployment or air-gapped deployment, depending on their infrastructure and security needs.

Best for

Bifrost is worth considering for enterprises that need centralized control over model access, spending, and AI tool interactions. It is especially relevant when performance, deployment control, and MCP governance are important alongside multi-provider routing.

Teams should still validate published performance claims against their own workloads and evaluate which enterprise capabilities they require.

2. LiteLLM: A Flexible Open-Source LLM Proxy

LiteLLM is an open-source project that provides a consistent interface for working with a wide range of LLM providers. It offers a Python SDK and a proxy server that teams can deploy as their own gateway.

This makes it useful for engineering teams that want to standardize model access without committing every application to a single provider. Developers can integrate through a common interface while managing provider connections and gateway configuration centrally.

What stands out

LiteLLM offers several features for teams building their own AI infrastructure:

  • Unified provider interface: Use a consistent API across supported model providers.
  • SDK and proxy options: Choose between integrating the Python SDK or running a gateway service.
  • Authentication and virtual keys: Centralize credentials and control access to configured deployments.
  • Usage and cost tracking: Monitor model usage and associate costs with different consumers.
  • Routing and fallbacks: Configure how requests are distributed across supported deployments and how failures are handled.

One of LiteLLM's main advantages is flexibility. Teams can inspect the implementation, customize their configuration, and deploy the proxy in infrastructure they control.

That flexibility also means the team must plan for maintenance, monitoring, scaling, and security. The amount of operational work depends on the architecture and deployment.

Explore the LiteLLM documentation for its SDK, proxy configuration, and supported integrations.

Best for

LiteLLM is best suited for developers and engineering teams that want an open-source, customizable gateway with broad provider compatibility. It is particularly useful for teams that prefer to manage their own infrastructure and want centralized authentication, routing, and cost visibility.

3. Kong AI Gateway: Extending API Management to AI

Kong AI Gateway extends the broader Kong Gateway platform with AI-specific routing, security, and observability capabilities.

For organizations that already use Kong to manage APIs, this can be a natural way to bring AI traffic into an existing governance model instead of introducing an entirely separate infrastructure layer.

What stands out

Kong's approach builds on established API management concepts:

  • Provider abstraction: Route requests to supported LLM providers through a common layer.
  • Centralized credentials: Manage provider access rather than distributing credentials across applications.
  • Routing and load balancing: Configure how AI requests are sent to upstream services.
  • Security policies: Apply authentication and access controls through the gateway.
  • AI observability: Track request activity and usage through the platform's monitoring capabilities.
  • MCP support: Its AI Gateway documentation includes MCP server management and related controls.

A major advantage is that AI traffic can be managed alongside existing API infrastructure. Teams may already have deployment processes, security policies, and operational expertise around Kong, reducing the need to establish a separate platform.

However, organizations that do not already use Kong should assess the learning curve and infrastructure overhead. They should also check which AI-specific capabilities are available in their chosen edition.

Best for

Kong AI Gateway is particularly relevant to enterprises that already rely on Kong and want to extend their API management practices to LLMs, MCP servers, and AI agents. It is less compelling to adopt solely for AI routing if the organization has no existing need for the broader Kong platform.

4. Cloudflare AI Gateway: AI Traffic Management at the Edge

Cloudflare AI Gateway provides a managed layer for observing and controlling AI application traffic. It fits naturally into environments where Cloudflare is already part of the application's networking or security infrastructure.

Rather than requiring teams to build their own monitoring and traffic-management components, it offers a set of features designed to make AI requests easier to observe and control.

What stands out

Cloudflare AI Gateway includes capabilities such as:

  • Analytics and logging: Inspect request activity, token usage, errors, and costs.
  • Caching: Serve eligible repeated requests from cache.
  • Rate limiting: Control request volume within configured limits.
  • Retries and fallbacks: Improve resilience when requests fail, where configured and supported.
  • Provider connectivity: Work with supported AI providers through the gateway.

Its integration with the wider Cloudflare ecosystem is a practical benefit for teams already using its infrastructure. The managed model also reduces the burden of operating a separate gateway service.

There are trade-offs. Teams must evaluate the service's deployment model, data handling, logging retention, and governance capabilities against their requirements. Organizations that need to operate the gateway entirely within their own infrastructure should pay particular attention to deployment constraints.

Best for

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a sensible option for teams already using Cloudflare that want visibility and basic traffic controls without managing another self-hosted service. It is particularly attractive when analytics, caching, rate limiting, and integration with existing infrastructure are the main priorities.

5. OpenRouter: Unified Access to a Broad Model Catalog

OpenRouter focuses on making a broad catalog of AI models accessible through a unified API. Instead of integrating separately with each supported provider, developers can use one interface to experiment with and access different models.

This approach is useful when teams are comparing models, building prototypes, or developing applications that may need to switch between different model families over time.

What stands out

OpenRouter emphasizes convenient access to a broad model ecosystem:

  • Broad model catalog: Discover and access models from different providers through one interface.
  • Unified API: Reduce the need to build separate integrations for each supported model.
  • Model selection: Choose models according to the capabilities and requirements of an application.
  • Provider routing: Use supported routing options to select among available provider routes.
  • Fallback capabilities: Configure supported alternatives for handling certain provider availability issues.

The main attraction is the ability to experiment with different models without maintaining a separate integration for every provider. This can simplify early development and make model comparisons easier.

OpenRouter is primarily a managed model-access service, so teams with strict requirements around private deployment, data handling, or internal infrastructure control should review whether its operating model fits their needs.

Explore the OpenRouter model catalog to see the available models and provider options.

Best for

OpenRouter is best suited for developers who want convenient access to a broad selection of models through one API. It is particularly useful for model experimentation, comparing different options, and building applications where flexibility in model selection is a priority.

How the Five LLM Gateways Compare

The table below summarizes their primary positioning. Feature availability can vary by edition, deployment, and configuration, so use it as a starting point rather than a substitute for checking current documentation.

Gateway Primary strength Routing Governance and cost controls Deployment approach
Bifrost Enterprise AI gateway with MCP capabilities Multi-provider routing and fallback Virtual keys, budgets, access controls Open-source and self-hosted options; enterprise deployment options
LiteLLM Flexible multi-provider proxy Provider and model routing Usage tracking, budgets, rate limits Open-source, self-hosted proxy
Kong AI Gateway API management extended to AI AI proxy and configurable routing API policies and AI governance features Self-hosted and managed options
Cloudflare AI Gateway Managed AI traffic management Provider connectivity and configured fallbacks Analytics, rate limiting, usage visibility Managed Cloudflare service
OpenRouter Broad model access Provider selection and fallback options Centralized access and billing; assess enterprise requirements Managed service

Comparing Them by Use Case

Sometimes it is easier to choose a gateway by starting with the problem you need to solve.

Your main requirement Gateway to evaluate Why
Monitoring and governing AI requests Bifrost Combines model routing with governance, usage controls, observability, and MCP gateway capabilities
Open-source gateway with customizable deployment Bifrost or LiteLLM Both provide open-source options; compare their routing, governance, ecosystem, and deployment requirements
AI traffic managed through existing API infrastructure Kong AI Gateway Extends Kong's established API management approach to AI
Managed analytics and traffic controls in a Cloudflare environment Cloudflare AI Gateway Provides caching, rate limiting, logs, and request resilience features
Easy access to many models for experimentation OpenRouter Centralizes model discovery and access across providers

The important distinction is that these products overlap without being interchangeable. A gateway that makes model experimentation easy may not provide the deployment control or governance depth an enterprise needs. Likewise, an organization already operating a mature API platform may value integration with its existing infrastructure more than a separate model-routing interface.

What Makes an LLM Gateway Production-Ready?

A gateway can simplify development, but production readiness depends on how well it handles the realities of running AI workloads.

Reliability: Provider failures and rate limits are inevitable. Understand how the gateway handles retries and fallback behavior, and whether it can route requests to suitable alternatives without creating unexpected costs or changing application behavior.

Performance: Measure the gateway's overhead under realistic traffic. Consider not only average latency but also tail latency, throughput, streaming behavior, and the impact of multiple sequential calls in agentic workflows.

Governance: Teams need to know who is using models, how much they are spending, and which policies apply. Look for controls that match your organizational structure, including per-user or per-team limits where required.

Observability: Request-level visibility helps developers investigate failures and understand usage patterns. Check which metrics, logs, and integrations are available, and how sensitive prompt or response data is handled.

Deployment and security: Consider where requests are processed, how credentials are stored, what data is retained, and whether the deployment model satisfies internal security and compliance requirements.

A feature checklist is useful, but a small proof of concept is often more revealing. Test the gateway using the models, request patterns, traffic levels, and policies your application will actually use.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an LLM gateway and an API gateway?

A traditional API gateway manages API traffic through functions such as authentication, routing, and rate limiting. An LLM gateway adds model-oriented capabilities such as provider selection, token usage tracking, model-specific fallback behavior, and AI cost management.

Do I need an LLM gateway if I use only one model provider?

Not necessarily. A direct integration may be sufficient for a small application, but a gateway can still help centralize logging, budgets, authentication, and rate limits. The decision depends on whether those operational benefits justify another layer in your architecture.

Which LLM gateways support open-source or self-hosted deployment?

Bifrost and LiteLLM provide open-source options, while Kong offers open-source gateway components alongside additional commercial capabilities. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter are primarily managed services, so verify each platform's current deployment options and licensing before deciding.

Can an LLM gateway reduce AI costs?

It can help by providing usage visibility, enforcing budgets, routing requests to suitable models, and caching eligible responses. Actual savings depend on the workload, provider pricing, cache hit rates, and how routing policies are configured.

Can an LLM gateway manage MCP traffic as well as LLM requests?

Some platforms support both, but their capabilities differ. Bifrost and Kong document MCP gateway functionality, while teams evaluating LiteLLM or other gateways should check the current scope of their MCP support and whether it provides the controls they need.

How should I choose the best LLM gateway for my team?

Start by identifying your biggest requirement: model flexibility, production reliability, governance, deployment control, or integration with existing infrastructure. Then compare the relevant capabilities, validate any important performance claims, and test your leading options against a representative workload.

Final Thoughts

Choosing an LLM gateway is less about finding a universally superior product and more about finding the right operational fit.

LiteLLM offers a flexible route for teams that want an open-source proxy, Kong makes sense when AI traffic needs to fit into an established API management environment, Cloudflare AI Gateway simplifies traffic management for Cloudflare users, and OpenRouter makes access to a broad model catalog straightforward.

Bifrost is particularly worth evaluating when the requirement extends beyond model access to enterprise governance, performance, and MCP tool management in a unified gateway.

Before committing, test the options against your actual workload and confirm that their security, deployment, and governance features meet your needs. If you'd like to see how Bifrost could fit into your AI infrastructure, book a demo with the Bifrost team.

articles.title: A 9.2 unauthenticated RCE in PHP: the audit, the patch window, and the offline switch
articles.description: CERT-EU says sites that can't patch should go offline: two 9.2 flaws in PHP itself, unauthenticated RCE, every version since PHP 5 possibly affected. The audit, the watch, and the offline switch — runnable receipts for the emergency window.
articles.body_html:
An EU cyber agency is telling websites they may need to be taken offline. Not patched later. Not monitored. Offline. The runtime that powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and most of the shared hosting internet has two 9.2-rated flaws — unauthenticated remote code execution — and the patch lands today at 14:00 GMT.

On Wednesday, the PHP security team releases fixes for two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale. Reuters reports what the agencies and vendors are saying around it — and the short version is that this is as serious as web emergencies get:

  • CERT-EU: the 9.2 rating indicates a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution — code running on your server without login. Their guidance: prepare for immediate patching, and those unable to patch should take affected sites offline.
  • ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre): identify every PHP system in your environment, prepare to patch, monitor for exploitation. Currently not aware of active exploitation — currently.
  • GoDaddy: the flaws could allow code execution over the internet — data theft, defacement, full system compromise.
  • Huntress: "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood."
  • Scope: all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected. Details, affected versions and fixed releases publish when the patch drops at 14:00 GMT today.

If that sounds dramatic for a language release, it is — and it should be. This is not a plugin bug or a framework edge case. It is the runtime itself.

Why this breaks the grading system

I grade controls on this blog in levels: what a control sees, who wrote it, what it survives. A Level 1 control is visible and bypassable; the quiz-hook post was one. The level below that is the ground the levels stand on: the runtime. Your WAF rules, your input validation, your hardening checklist — every one of them is PHP executing your defense. An unauthenticated RCE in PHP is an attack on the level that decides what "executing" means.

Monday I wrote about Rust's memory-safety proof — an 11-year-old hole exposing the premise the proof rests on. Here is the mirror image: the most-deployed server language on the web, whose security model predates the modern threat model entirely, calling an emergency patch window while an EU agency briefs the offline switch. Two runtimes, two philosophies, same week — and both stories are the same story: the premise is part of the proof.

Run it yourself: the audit, the watch, the switch

The details of the vulnerability are withheld until the patch lands — so the receipts that matter right now are the ones on your side. Three pipelines:

1. The inventory — find every PHP on the machines you control:

# what's installed (Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL families)
dpkg -l | grep -E "php[0-9.]*-" | awk '{print $2, $3}'
rpm -qa | grep -E "^php" | sort

# what actually executes, and since when
php -v 2>/dev/null; php-fpm -v 2>/dev/null

# every PHP binary on disk, including the ones a panel installed years ago
sudo find / -name "php*" -type f -perm -111 2>/dev/null | grep -vE "/proc|/sys" | head -20

That last command is the one that finds the forgotten PHP 5.6 sitting in a panel directory that nobody has touched since 2019 — the exact asset CERT-EU's advisory exists for.

2. The exposure — what faces the internet right now:

# php-fpm sockets and pools
ss -tlnp | grep -E "php|9000"
# every vhost routing to PHP
grep -rE "php|fastcgi" /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/ 2>/dev/null | wc -l

3. The watch — until the patch lands, the exploit probes are your tripwire. You don't know the signature yet, so watch the volume and the weirdness:

# requests hitting PHP endpoints, last hour, with response codes
awk -v d="$(date -d '1 hour ago' '+%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M')" '$0 ~ d' /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  | grep -E "\.php" | awk '{print $1, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

Spikes of POSTs to .php paths on sites that have no PHP forms, or 200s from paths that should 404 — that is your "currently not aware of active exploitation" turning into "aware."

4. The switch — when the patch drops at 14:00 GMT:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade "php*"
sudo systemctl restart php8.3-fpm   # your version
php -v                                # confirm the new release

And the offline switch CERT-EU is briefing — for assets you cannot patch in the window:

sudo systemctl stop php8.3-fpm
# serve a static maintenance page with no PHP in the path:
# nginx: return 503 with a maintenance root; the runtime is out of the request path entirely.

Stopping php-fpm removes the runtime from the request path — no PHP executing, no PHP vulnerability executing. It is the crudest control in this post and the only one CERT-EU explicitly endorsed for the unpatchable.

What you actually get

  • A deadline: 14:00 GMT today. The details land with the patch; the audit above is everything you can do before reading them.
  • A decision tree: can patch in the window → patch and verify the version. Can't patch → the offline switch, or take the asset off the internet edge. Don't know if you're exposed → the inventory commands exist for exactly that.
  • The honest limits: nothing in this post tells you whether you're vulnerable to these specific flaws — PHP publishes that when the patch lands. What the audit tells you is where every PHP lives, which is the prerequisite for patching in minutes instead of days.

And the premise note, because it's the same week: memory safety in the runtime is not an academic property. Eleven years of a proof on one side, an EU offline advisory on the other. The language your server runs is your attack surface's foundation — everything above it is scaffolding.

The patch drops at 14:00 GMT. The audit takes ten minutes. Do the audit first.

Sources: Reuters — EU agency warns websites may need to be taken offline as PHP prepares patches (Oct 21, 2026 — quoting CERT-EU, ACSC, GoDaddy, Huntress, PHP security team). The runtime-as-premise framing follows my Rust memory-safety post. Watch this post's dev.to comments — I'll update with the CVE details and fixed versions after the 14:00 GMT release.

articles.title: Get Your Free got-a.page Subdomain: A Step-by-Step Guide
articles.description: I recently bought the domain got-a.page and turned it into a free, community-run subdomain service....
articles.body_html:
I recently bought the domain got-a.page and turned it into a free, community-run subdomain service. Anyone can claim a name like yourname.got-a.page with one small JSON file and one pull request. No hosting bill, no registrar account, no ads, no tracking.

This guide walks through the whole thing: picking a name, choosing a mode, opening the PR, and what to expect after it merges.

What is got-a.page?

got-a.page gives you a free subdomain for your profile, product, project or community. Claims live in a public GitHub repo, one JSON file per page, and a maintainer merges them. There are two ways to use your name:

Instant mode - no website? We host the page for you.
Fill in your name, a tagline and your links, and a fast, accessible page is rendered at yourname.got-a.page. Light and dark mode included, in one of six themes: sunrise, lagoon, forest, plum, slate, ember. Person and product pages are supported today.

{
  "mode": "instant",
  "owner": { "github": "yourusername" },
  "page": {
    "type": "person",
    "title": "Your Name",
    "tagline": "What you're about, in one line",
    "avatar": "https://github.com/yourusername.png",
    "theme": "sunrise",
    "links": [{ "label": "GitHub", "url": "https://github.com/yourusername" }],
    "sections": [{ "heading": "About", "text": "A few sentences about you." }]
  }
}

Point mode - already hosting somewhere?
Point your name at GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or anywhere that gives you a hostname or IP. CNAME, A, AAAA and TXT records are supported. One DNS rule to know: a CNAME can't be combined with other record types on the same name.

{
  "mode": "point",
  "owner": { "github": "yourusername" },
  "purpose": "My portfolio",
  "records": { "CNAME": "yourusername.github.io" }
}

You can switch modes later by editing your file with a new PR. And yes, it's really free: the domain is paid for years ahead and everything else runs on free tiers.

Before you start

  • A GitHub account. Claims are tied to it: owner.github must match the PR author, and only you (or a maintainer) can edit or remove your page later.
  • A name that's 2-40 characters of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens.
  • Up to 2 pages per GitHub account while we're young.
  • Everything in the repo is public, forever. Don't put private data in your file.

Step 1: Open the guided claim form

Go to got-a.page/claim. The form writes the JSON for you, so you never touch raw JSON. There's a name checker on the homepage if you want to see whether your name is free first.

Step 2: Answer a few questions

Enter your page name, pick instant or point mode, and fill in the fields. Instant mode asks for your title, tagline, theme and links. Point mode asks for the DNS target your host recommends.

Step 3: Propose it on GitHub

The button at the end opens the claim repo on GitHub with your file prefilled. GitHub will ask you to fork (one click), then you choose "Propose changes" and open the pull request.

Automated validation checks review your file. Follow the check results on your PR - fork PRs don't get automatic bot comments, so the checks are where the feedback lives. A maintainer merges when it looks good.

Never made a pull request before? The repo's contributing guide walks you through every click. It's a kind place for your first one.

Step 4 (point mode only): connect your host before merge

This is the step people miss. A merged claim creates DNS records, but it does not add the domain to your hosting account. Add yourname.got-a.page on your host before the claim is merged:

  • GitHub Pages: your website repo > Settings > Pages > Custom domain, enter yourname.got-a.page, Save. Use "records": { "CNAME": "yourusername.github.io" } in your claim.
  • Vercel: your project > Settings > Domains > Add Domain. Copy the project-specific CNAME target Vercel gives you into your claim.
  • Netlify: Domain management > Add a domain you already own. Keep external DNS and copy the recommended target (usually your-site.netlify.app).
  • Cloudflare Pages: your Pages project > Custom domains > Set up a domain. Use your your-site.pages.dev target.

The docs at got-a.page/docs have the full per-host walkthrough.

What to expect after your PR merges

Instant mode: your page goes live within a few minutes. Until the index republishes, your address may still show the "unclaimed" page - that's normal, give it a few minutes and hard-refresh.

Point mode: DNS publishes first, then your host verifies the domain and issues its HTTPS certificate. Browsers will show a privacy or certificate error for your address during that window. That's expected - minutes to hours, occasionally longer. GitHub documents up to 24 hours for Enforce HTTPS to become available; turn it on once you can.

One HTTPS note: .page is on the HSTS preload list, so browsers force HTTPS on every got-a.page address. Instant pages are always secure (handled for you), and point-mode targets must serve valid HTTPS or browsers will refuse to load them. All the hosts above do that automatically once the custom domain is added.

"Is it broken?" - troubleshooting

What you see What's going on
Certificate/privacy error right after merge (point mode) Normal. Your host's certificate isn't ready yet. Wait, then enable Enforce HTTPS when offered.
Your old yourname.github.io shows the same error Expected. GitHub Pages redirects the old address to your custom domain as soon as you save it, so both show the error during the wait and both recover together.
Your address still says "unclaimed" (instant mode) The index hasn't republished yet. A few minutes, then hard-refresh.
Page loads but looks unstyled Your site is loading CSS/JS from the old address or over http://. Use relative asset URLs or update your static site generator's base URL setting.
Still stuck after a day Open an issue in the claim repo with your page name and what you see. Real humans read them.

The rules, short version

  • Claim with your own GitHub account.
  • Your page is public. Everything in the repo is public.
  • No phishing, scams, malware, impersonation, illegal or adult content.
  • Some names are reserved (service addresses, brand names, and words that would make the place less welcoming).
  • See abuse? Email abuse@got-a.page.

Extras

Badges: once your page is live, grab an "I got a page" or "Launched on got-a.page" badge from got-a.page/badges - HTML and Markdown snippets, ready to paste into your README.

What's coming later: more page types (project, community and event templates), a Wall of Pages gallery, and email on your subdomain. None of that is live yet - I'm adding it in later phases, and everything above is what works today.

Wrap up

  1. Check your name on got-a.page
  2. Claim it at got-a.page/claim
  3. Open the PR, follow the checks, done

Claim repo: github.com/got-a-page/claim - MIT licensed, and issues and first PRs are welcome. If you claim a page, drop your new address in the comments. I'd love to see what you make of it.

articles.title: How to Keep Billing State Correct When Webhook Events Repeat, Arrive Late, or Fail
articles.description: When building apps in production, the billing provider you decide to use tells your app what happened...
articles.body_html:
When building apps in production, the billing provider you decide to use tells your app what happened to a customer, such as a payment that succeeded, a plan that changed, or a subscription that ended. Your app then turns each message into a change in its own database: a plan column, a monthly allowance, or a flag that lets someone in.

Those messages travel over a network that duplicates, delays and drops, so the same payment message can arrive three times, a cancellation can arrive after the upgrade that replaced it, and a server can stop half way through a message. Each case goes on to corrupt a customer's state in a different way, and none of them shows up when you test with one clean message.

Which brings me to a question a developer friend of mine asked me last week: how does an app keep a customer's plan and allowance correct when the events that change them can repeat, arrive out of order, or stop in the middle?

This post builds the answer as a small pipeline: an endpoint that stores each event before it answers, a queue in Postgres that holds the stored events, and a worker that applies them with effects that are safe to repeat.

To show this in practice, I built an example app called "Bottle", it's a reminder app with a free plan and a paid plan using Kinde under the hood to send billing events.

Kinde is a platform for authentication and billing, and here it is the billing provider whose plan and payment changes the app must follow. After building the app, I tested the pipeline against the events Kinde sent for my own account and I'll be breaking it all down in this article.

What goes wrong when a handler applies each message as it arrives

First, we will start with the handler most apps write, which reads the message, changes the database, and answers 200 (OK). That works on a quiet day with a clean network, but three things can potentially break it.

The same event arrives more than once. If the app applies a payment and the 200 answer never reaches the provider, the provider sends the payment again. The handler adds the monthly allowance a second time. And will do the same a third time if a third copy arrives.

An old event arrives after a newer one. A customer upgrades, so the old plan is cancelled. The cancellation happened first, but a retry delays it, and it arrives last. A handler that only trusts the order of arrival will set the customer back to Free.

The server stops in the middle. A plan change needs two writes: the plan, then the allowance that goes with it. If the process stops between them, the customer is on Pro with a Free balance. The provider retries, but by then the state is already split.

I wrote a handler that applies each message on arrival and ran nine deliveries of three events through it. The nine are the plan change three times, the payment five times, and one old cancellation. The worker stops once during the first plan change, and this is what the account looked like along the way:

  • After delivery 2, the plan was Pro and the balance was still 10, because the process stopped before the allowance write.
  • After delivery 7, the plan was Free, because the old cancellation arrived last and won.
  • After delivery 9, the balance was 2,950. The correct balance is 500.

The account ended on Pro only because the plan change happened to arrive a third time. The handler had no rule that made it come out right, and the rest of this post builds those rules.

What the provider promises

A fix has to match what the provider actually does, so I read Kinde's webhook documentation before I designed anything. These are the parts that matter for correctness:

  • The body of each request is a JWT (a signed token) with the content type application/jwt. You check its signature against the keys Kinde publishes at /.well-known/jwks on your Kinde domain.
  • Every request carries a webhook-id header. Kinde describes it as unique to a webhook and an event, and the same on every attempt. The docs tell you to use it as the idempotency key.
  • A 200 answer means delivered. Any other answer, or no answer, makes Kinde try again.
  • The retry schedule is roughly: immediately, then after 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour and 4 hours, then every 12 hours until 36 hours have passed.
  • An endpoint that fails for 72 hours is disabled, and the account owner gets an email.

That list explains the three failures. The promise is "we keep trying until we hear 200", so a copy arrives whenever your 200 gets lost, even if your app applied the event correctly. A retry that waits 10 minutes also arrives after every event sent in those 10 minutes, which is how order is lost. The docs do not promise an order for events on one endpoint, and the retry schedule shows why no one could. The pipeline assumes no order and expects copies.

The event itself carries what the handler needs. Here is a customer.plan_changed event from my account, with the fields I use and the rest left out:

{
  "type": "customer.plan_changed",
  "event_id": "event_01a1…",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-21T02:29:24.481368869+11:00",
  "event_timestamp": "2026-10-21T02:29:23.403633+11:00",
  "data": {
    "user_id": "kp_4940…",
    "customer_id": "customer_0198…",
    "customer_type": "user",
    "plan": { "key": "customer_pro_plan" }
  }
}

The plan is an object, and its key is at data.plan.key. The user and customer ids tell the handler which account to change. The two timestamps matter later, in the section on ordering.

The pipeline

The design follows from two facts. An event can arrive many times, so the app needs one stored copy and a counter. An event can also arrive at any time, so the app must apply it in a way that does not depend on when. Four rules do that work.

Rule 1: Store the event, then answer

The endpoint does three things and nothing else: it checks the signature, writes the event to a table, and answers 200. Applying the event happens after the answer.

If the signature is not valid, the endpoint answers 401 and stores nothing. If the database write fails, the endpoint answers with an error, and Kinde tries again later. The 200 therefore means one thing: the event is stored. It does not mean the event is applied. That difference is what lets Bottle survive a crash, because a stored event can run again and a lost event cannot.

The signature check is one call to the jose library, which fetches Kinde's keys once and caches them. After the check, the event goes into inbox_events:

INSERT INTO inbox_events (source, dedupe_key, type, payload, occurred_at, …)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4::jsonb, $5, …)
ON CONFLICT (source, dedupe_key)
DO UPDATE SET seen_count = inbox_events.seen_count + 1
RETURNING id, (xmax = 0) AS inserted

Rule 2: One key for each event

The webhook-id header is the dedupe key, and the table has a unique constraint on it. The first copy inserts a row. Every later copy hits the conflict, adds one to seen_count, and does nothing else.

The last line of the query tells the caller which case happened. In Postgres, xmax is 0 for a row the statement just created, so (xmax = 0) is true only for a new event. Bottle also writes one row to a receipts table for every delivery. That gives the app a record of all nine copies even though only three events exist.

I considered keeping seen ids in memory or in a cache. Both lose the ids when the process restarts, and a restart is exactly when copies arrive. The key has to live in the same database as the event.

Rule 3: Apply each event in one transaction, with a lease

A worker claims stored events and applies them. Two workers can run at once, for example when the endpoint starts one after its answer and a timer starts another, and they must not take the same event, so the claim uses a clause Postgres provides for this:

UPDATE inbox_events
   SET status = 'processing', attempts = attempts + 1,
       locked_until = now() + interval '30 seconds'
 WHERE id IN (
   SELECT id FROM inbox_events
    WHERE (status IN ('received', 'failed') AND next_attempt_at <= now())
       OR (status = 'processing' AND locked_until < now())
    ORDER BY occurred_at, id
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT 25)
RETURNING *

SKIP LOCKED makes a second worker pass over rows the first worker holds. The 30-second lease handles a worker that dies. When the lease ends, the row is claimed again.

The worker then runs the handler and marks the event applied inside one transaction. Either both happen or neither does. If the process stops half way, the database rolls back, and the event runs again from the start. That removes the third failure from the list, because the plan write and the allowance write can no longer be separated.

When a handler throws, the event goes back to failed and waits. The waits are 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes and 1 hour. After six attempts the event is marked dead, which keeps it visible without running it forever.

I chose Postgres over a message queue for one reason. The claim, the effect and the mark must share a transaction, and a separate queue cannot join one. Billing events are also low in volume, so one more service would add cost without adding safety.

Rule 4: Make every effect safe to repeat

The first three rules reduce how often a handler runs twice, but only this rule makes a second run harmless, and it has to protect two effects.

The allowance is a ledger row, and the row has a key made of the account and the month. Writing it again does nothing:

INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, period, delta, reason, entry_key)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, 'pro:' || $1 || ':' || $2)
ON CONFLICT (entry_key) DO NOTHING

Both the payment handler and the plan change handler try to write this same row. Whichever event arrives first grants the Pro allowance, and the other finds the row and skips it. That is why a payment that arrives before its plan change does no harm. The plan change grants the allowance when it comes.

The plan has its own protection, and it depends on time rather than arrival.

Arrival order is not the order things happened

Each stored event has an occurred_at time taken from the event, not from the moment the copy arrived. A plan change applies only if its time is newer than the plan change already stored:

UPDATE accounts SET plan = $2, plan_changed_at = $3
 WHERE id = $1 AND plan_changed_at < $3
RETURNING id

If the update changes no row, the handler records ignored: a newer plan change is already stored and stops.

The diagram shows the effect. The cancellation happened three minutes before the upgrade, but it arrives seventh. The database already holds a newer plan change, so the cancellation does nothing and the customer stays on Pro.

The event has two timestamps. In the two events I stored, event_timestamp was about one second earlier than timestamp. I read the first as the time of the change and the second as the time Kinde sent the message. Bottle uses event_timestamp when it is present and falls back to timestamp. The choice matters, because the guard compares times, and a time that means "when it was sent" would reorder events that were sent late.

Replay and ignored events

Two features come from the same idea: a stored event is a fact you can look at again.

An ignored event keeps its reason. When a handler chooses to do nothing, it writes why. The log shows "ignored: a newer plan change is already stored", not a silent skip. An event the handler cannot use shows up the same way.

A replay puts a stored event back in the queue. It sets the status to received and lets the worker run it again. Replay is safe because of Rule 4. A replayed payment finds its ledger row and writes nothing. A replayed plan change finds a newer change and is ignored. Replay is how you run stored events again after a handler changes or after an outage, and it needs no new code path.

In Bottle, each billing event on the account page has a Replay link. The route behind it only accepts events that belong to the signed-in account, because replay should not let one customer requeue another customer's events.

What happened with live events

The tests cover the rules, but I also wanted events sent by Kinde itself. In Kinde, I moved my own user from Pro to the Starter plan and back to Pro. Kinde sent the events to Bottle's live endpoint. To test a late delivery, I then replayed the older Starter change after the Pro change had applied.

The log on the account page shows the result in the screenshot above. The Pro change reads "plan set to pro, Pro allowance granted". The older Starter change reads "ignored: a newer plan change is already stored". The account shows the Pro plan and 500 bottles for the month.

The same nine deliveries from the first section run through the pipeline on Bottle's Engine Room page. The page uses the same intake code and handlers as the live endpoint, on a fresh test account each time.

The numbers are these:

  • 9 copies arrived and 3 events were stored. The other 6 copies were counted and dropped.
  • 1 plan change stopped in the middle. It stayed stored, and the next copy ran it to the end.
  • The late cancellation was ignored, because a newer plan change was stored.
  • The account ended on Pro with a balance of 500, and the allowance was granted once.

The handler that applies on arrival ended with 2,950. That is 2,450 more bottles than the plan allows, and nothing in the database records how they got there.

Limits

This design has edges.

  • Order depends on the provider's clock. The guard compares event times from Kinde. Two plan changes with the same timestamp are treated as a tie, and the second one is ignored.
  • The live log shows two event types. The plan change and the cancellation came from real Kinde events. The payment handlers and the overdue-invoice handler follow the documented event names and are covered by tests, but I did not watch Kinde send them.
  • The token's timestamp has no age limit. Kinde's docs mention checking the timestamp for replay protection. Bottle does not reject old tokens. The dedupe table already refuses a second copy of any webhook-id, but it does not expire a token.
  • A dead event needs a person. After six attempts, an event is marked dead and stays visible. Bottle does not page anyone. A production system needs an alert on that status.
