  • Postgres is the queue. It suits the low volume of billing events. A stream of millions of events a day is a job for a message queue.

The rule that holds it together

The stored event is the fact, and a delivery is one attempt to tell you about it. Once the app treats it that way, a copy becomes a counter, a late event becomes a comparison of times, and a crash becomes a retry. None of the three needs special code, because each one is the same case: a stored event that has not been applied yet.

To run it yourself, clone the repository, run npm test for the 23 tests, and run npm run dev for the app. The Engine Room page runs the nine deliveries in your browser.

After testing it out yourself, do drop a comment below telling me your findings, even if you test it with a completely different billing provider.

FAQ

Why answer 200 before the event is applied?
The provider stops retrying once it hears 200. Applying an event can be slow or can fail. If the app answers only after applying, every failure becomes a retry of an event that may be half applied. Storing first makes the answer fast and keeps the event safe.

Which key should I dedupe on?
Use the key the provider documents. For Kinde, that is the webhook-id header, which stays the same across attempts. Store it with a unique constraint in the same database as the event.

Can I use a queue like SQS instead of Postgres?
Yes, but the claim, the effect and the "applied" mark can no longer share one transaction. You then need the effects to be safe to repeat on their own, which Rule 4 requires anyway.

How do I test retries and reordering?
Write down a sequence of deliveries that includes copies, a late event and a crash, and run it against the handler. The Engine Room page does this, and the repository has the same sequence as a test.

articles.title: A liquid glass tab bar: the magnifying lens is a scaled copy of the bar
articles.description: How the lens in a liquid glass tab bar magnifies the icon under it without SVG filters, and how a spring's velocity stretches it like a drop. Plain HTML/CSS/JS demo, plus the Framer Motion version.
articles.body_html:
Apple's liquid glass tab bars have a lens that sits on the selected tab and magnifies the icon under it. When you switch tabs it moves like a drop of water: it stretches on the way, then settles.

Most web versions of this effect use an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter. That only renders in Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox skip it. I built one for a music-app demo and wanted it to look the same in every browser, so the lens uses no filter at all. It's a small window onto a second copy of the bar, scaled up 1.42 times.

This post covers three pieces:

  1. The glass bar (plain backdrop-filter).
  2. The lens: a clipped, scaled copy, and the one line of math that keeps it lined up.
  3. The drop: a spring whose speed sets the lens width.

There's a single-file demo at the end you can paste into CodePen. If you build with Cursor or Claude Code, it also works as a reference file to hand to your agent: it's short, and every number in it is explained here.

1. The glass bar

The bar itself is ordinary frosted glass. Blur plus saturation does most of the work. The inset shadows draw a light top edge and a faint 1px rim so the bar reads as a solid object on any background.

This is the CSS from the shipped component (tabbar-liquid.css):

.glassbar {
  position: absolute;
  border-radius: 32px;
  background: var(--glass);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22),
    inset 0 0 0 1px var(--glass-line),
    0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45);
}

saturate(1.9) matters more than it looks. Blur alone washes colours out to grey. Saturation brings back the colour of whatever scrolls underneath, which is what makes it read as glass and not as a grey panel.

Keep the -webkit- prefix. Safari still wants it.

2. The lens is a copy, not a filter

Real magnification would need a displacement filter on whatever sits behind the lens. You can fake the part people actually notice, the icon under the lens getting bigger, with plain transforms:

  • Render the tabs a second time inside the lens element.
  • Give the lens overflow: hidden so you only see the part under it.
  • Scale the copy by M (1.42 here) around the lens centre.

The markup is a lens with an inner layer that holds the copy:

<div class="lens" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="lensIn"><!-- the same tabs again, not focusable --></div>
</div>

The copy must stay out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, or a screen reader reads every tab twice. In the React component the copy is rendered with live={false}, which does exactly that:

const inert = live ? {} : { tabIndex: -1, 'aria-hidden': true as const };

The one line of math

.lensIn has transform-origin: 0 0 and fills the same box as the real bar. The lens has width w, height h, and centre (x, y) in bar coordinates, so its top-left corner is (lx, ly) = (x - w/2, y - h/2).

You want the point under the lens centre to stay where it is, with everything around it pushed outwards by M. Here's the render code from the shipped engine.ts:

const Ls = S.lens, lx = Ls.x - Ls.w / 2, ly = Ls.y - Ls.h / 2, M = 1.42;
lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx.toFixed(1)}px,${ly.toFixed(1)}px) scale(${Ls.sx.toFixed(4)},${Ls.sy.toFixed(4)})`;
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${(-lx + Ls.x - M * Ls.x).toFixed(2)}px,${(-ly + Ls.y - M * Ls.y).toFixed(2)}px) scale(${M})`;

Why it works: a point p of the copy lands at M·p + t inside the lens, and the lens sits at lx. On screen that is lx + M·p + (-lx + x - M·x), which simplifies to x + M·(p - x). At p = x you get x, so the centre stays put and everything else spreads out from it by M. It's the textbook "scale around a point" transform, with the lens offset cancelled out.

Since the copy is real DOM, you can style it apart from the bar. Trimmed from the shipped CSS (the comments are mine):

.lens {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; overflow: hidden; pointer-events: none;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,.07);
  backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75),     /* bright top rim */
    inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,244,50,.55),     /* lime bottom rim */
    inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
    inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35),    /* pink left edge */
    inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35),   /* cyan right edge */
    0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4),
    0 12px 28px rgba(0,0,0,.5),
    0 0 34px rgba(198,244,50,.42);
}
.lensIn { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
.lensIn .tab { color: var(--volt); }        /* the magnified icon turns lime */
.lensIn .tab i { opacity: 0 !important; }   /* hide the label inside the lens */
.lensIn .tab svg { translate: 0 8px; }      /* and drop the icon into the middle */
.lensIn .dockc {
  filter: drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6))
          drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6));
}

Two details from that block:

  • The pink and cyan inset shadows on the left and right edges, plus two 1.6px drop-shadows on the copy, fake the colour fringing you see where real glass bends light. They're cheap and they sell the effect more than anything else in the file.
  • The label is hidden inside the lens and the icon moves down 8px. A magnified label gets cut off by the lens edge and looks like a bug. A centred icon looks deliberate.

The cost of this approach is that the content renders twice. For five icons that's nothing. The same component reuses the trick for a bigger orb that lifts out of the bar: the orb's copy holds the whole screen, scaled with the same formula.

3. The drop: speed sets the width

A lens that slides at a fixed width looks like a highlight pill. It reads as liquid once it stretches while it moves and goes back to round when it stops.

In the React version the lens x-position is a Framer Motion spring, and useVelocity reads how fast that spring is moving:

// live mode: the lens rides a spring, and its speed stretches the drop
const x = useSpring(tabX(0), { stiffness: 380, damping: 26 });
const stretch = useVelocity(x);

Every frame, the speed (px/s) maps to the lens size:

const v = Math.abs(stretch.get());
S.lens = {
  x: lx, y: g.cy,
  w: mix(66 + Math.min(92, v / 9), 56, c),
  h: mix(52 - Math.min(10, v / 90), 56, c),
  /* ... */
};

Leave out mix(..., c) for now. That's the compact state, when the bar shrinks on scroll. What's left:

  • At rest the lens is 66 × 52.
  • It gets 1px wider for every 9 px/s of speed, up to 92px more.
  • It gets thinner by up to 10px, so a fast move reads as a long, thin drop.
  • The clamps stop a very fast flick from stretching it across the whole bar.

The spring's overshoot does the rest. With stiffness 380 and damping 26 the spring is underdamped (damping ratio about 0.67), so it passes the target a little and comes back. The width follows the speed, so you get a wobble on landing without writing one keyframe.

Switching tabs is one line: x.set(tabX(i)).

Keyboard and screen readers

The real tabs are a tablist. Each tab gets role="tab" and aria-selected, and left/right arrows move between them:

if (e.key !== 'ArrowRight' && e.key !== 'ArrowLeft') return;
e.preventDefault(); i = (i + (e.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : 4)) % 5;
screen.current?.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-dock] [data-tab]')[i]?.focus();

(+ 4 is - 1 modulo 5, so left arrow from the first tab wraps to the last.)

The lens, the copy and the rings are all aria-hidden. Only the real tabs are announced.

The single-file version

No Framer Motion here. The spring is about ten lines of Hooke's law with damping, using the same stiffness and damping as the React version. Paste it into CodePen's HTML panel or save it as a .html file and open it:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
<title>Liquid glass tab bar: magnifying lens demo</title>
<!-- MIT licence. Teaching version of the lens from qodesign's Liquid Glass Tab Bar (qodesign.dev). -->
<style>
  :root { --ink:#0A0A0D; --text:#F4F4F6; --muted:#8A8FA3; --lime:#C6FF3D; }
  * { box-sizing:border-box; margin:0 }
  body { min-height:100vh; display:grid; place-items:center; background:#050507; font-family:system-ui,sans-serif; color:var(--text) }
  .phone { position:relative; width:390px; height:700px; max-width:100vw; border-radius:44px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink) }
  .feed { position:absolute; inset:0; overflow-y:auto; padding:56px 18px 140px; display:grid; gap:14px }
  .card { height:150px; border-radius:22px; display:flex; align-items:flex-end; padding:16px; font-weight:600 }
  .card:nth-child(3n+1) { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#8B6CFF,#2a1d66) }
  .card:nth-child(3n+2) { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#ff6a3d,#5a1d0b) }
  .card:nth-child(3n)   { background:linear-gradient(135deg,#C6FF3D,#2d4a00); color:#0A0A0D }

  /* the glass bar */
  .dock { position:absolute; left:14px; right:14px; bottom:22px; height:76px }
  .bar { position:absolute; inset:0; border-radius:32px; background:rgba(28,30,40,.45);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(16px) saturate(1.9); backdrop-filter:blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
    box-shadow:inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22), inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(255,255,255,.1), 0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45) }
  .tabs { position:absolute; inset:0; display:flex }
  .tab { flex:1; display:flex; flex-direction:column; align-items:center; justify-content:center; gap:3px;
    border:0; background:none; color:var(--muted); font:600 10.5px system-ui; border-radius:24px; cursor:pointer; touch-action:none }
  .tab svg { width:25px; height:25px; fill:none; stroke:currentColor; stroke-width:2; stroke-linecap:round; stroke-linejoin:round }
  .tab[aria-selected="true"] { color:var(--text) }
  .tab:focus-visible { outline:2px solid var(--lime); outline-offset:-4px }

  /* the lens: a window onto a scaled copy of the tabs */
  .lens { position:absolute; left:0; top:0; overflow:hidden; pointer-events:none; will-change:transform,width,height;
    background:rgba(255,255,255,.07);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18); backdrop-filter:blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
    box-shadow:inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75), inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,255,61,.55), inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
      inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35), inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35), 0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4), 0 0 34px rgba(198,255,61,.42) }
  .lens::after { content:""; position:absolute; left:14%; right:14%; top:5%; height:34%; border-radius:50%;
    background:linear-gradient(rgba(255,255,255,.5),rgba(255,255,255,0)) }
  .lensIn { position:absolute; left:0; top:0; transform-origin:0 0;
    filter:drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6)) drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6)) }
  .lensIn .tab { color:var(--lime) }
  .lensIn .tab span { opacity:0 }
  .lensIn .tab svg { translate:0 8px }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="phone">
  <div class="feed" aria-label="Feed">
    <div class="card">Daily mix</div><div class="card">Late night</div><div class="card">Focus</div>
    <div class="card">Running</div><div class="card">Vinyl finds</div><div class="card">Live sets</div>
  </div>
  <nav class="dock">
    <div class="bar"></div>
    <div class="tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="Sections" id="tabs"></div>
    <div class="lens" id="lens" aria-hidden="true"><div class="lensIn" id="lensIn"></div></div>
  </nav>
</div>
<script>
const TABS = [
  ['Home',    '<path d="M3 11l9-7 9 7v9a1 1 0 0 1-1 1h-5v-6H9v6H4a1 1 0 0 1-1-1z"/>'],
  ['Explore', '<circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9"/><path d="M15.5 8.5l-2 5-5 2 2-5z"/>'],
  ['Library', '<path d="M4 4v16M9 4v16M14 4l6 16"/>'],
  ['Inbox',   '<path d="M4 13l2-8h12l2 8v6H4z"/><path d="M4 13h5l1 2h4l1-2h5"/>'],
  ['Profile', '<circle cx="12" cy="8" r="4"/><path d="M4 21c1.5-4 4.5-6 8-6s6.5 2 8 6"/>'],
];
const tabHTML = (live) => TABS.map(([label, icon], i) =>
  `<button class="tab" type="button" ${live ? `role="tab" aria-selected="${i === 0}" tabindex="${i ? -1 : 0}"` : 'tabindex="-1"'}>
     <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">${icon}</svg><span>${label}</span></button>`).join('');

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const dock = document.querySelector('.dock'), tabsEl = $('tabs'), lens = $('lens'), lensIn = $('lensIn');
tabsEl.innerHTML = tabHTML(true);
lensIn.innerHTML = `<div class="tabs">${tabHTML(false)}</div>`;   // the copy the lens magnifies
const tabs = [...tabsEl.children];
const M = 1.42;                                                     // magnification
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const spring = { x: 0, v: 0, target: 0, k: 380, c: 26 };
const centerOf = (i) => tabs[i].offsetLeft + tabs[i].offsetWidth / 2;
let active = 0;

function select(i, focus) {
  active = (i + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
  tabs.forEach((t, j) => { t.setAttribute('aria-selected', j === active); t.tabIndex = j === active ? 0 : -1; });
  if (focus) tabs[active].focus();
  spring.target = centerOf(active);
  if (reduce.matches) { spring.x = spring.target; spring.v = 0; }
}

function paint() {
  const W = dock.clientWidth, H = dock.clientHeight;
  lensIn.style.width = W + 'px'; lensIn.style.height = H + 'px';
  const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);                        // px per second
  const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);                  // faster = longer drop
  const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);                 // ...and a little thinner
  const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));      // keep the drop inside the bar
  const y = H / 2, lx = x - w / 2, ly = y - h / 2;
  lens.style.width = w + 'px'; lens.style.height = h + 'px';
  lens.style.borderRadius = Math.min(w, h) / 2 + 'px';
  lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx}px, ${ly}px)`;
  // keep the point under the lens centre still, and scale everything around it
  lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;
}

let last = performance.now();
function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(0.032, (now - last) / 1000); last = now;
  const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;   // Hooke + damping, mass 1
  spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;
  paint();
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// tap, drag across the bar, or use the arrow keys
const nearest = (clientX) => {
  const r = dock.getBoundingClientRect(), px = clientX - r.left;
  return tabs.reduce((best, t, i) => Math.abs(centerOf(i) - px) < Math.abs(centerOf(best) - px) ? i : best, 0);
};
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { tabsEl.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => { if (e.buttons) select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') { e.preventDefault(); select(active + 1, true); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft')  { e.preventDefault(); select(active - 1, true); }
});
addEventListener('resize', () => { spring.target = spring.x = centerOf(active); });

spring.x = spring.target = centerOf(0);
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })

  • It clamps the drop inside the bar, because a 158px drop on the last tab hangs off the edge.
  • With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce it jumps straight to the new tab, with no stretch and no wobble. Do that in anything you ship. A drop that stretches across the screen is exactly the kind of motion that setting is for.

Easy ways to get it wrong

  • Scaling the copy around its own centre. The magnified icon drifts sideways as the lens moves. Use transform-origin: 0 0 and put the whole offset in the translate.
  • A CSS transition on the lens width. The width then lags behind the position. Set width, height and transform in the same frame, all read from the spring.

articles.title: AI Coding Tip 041 - Turn Every Review Finding Into a Rule
articles.description: A human should never address the same issue twice.   TL;DR: Turn every human review finding into a...
articles.body_html:
A human should never address the same issue twice.

TL;DR: Turn every human review finding into a harness rule, so the next review starts where this one ended.

Common Mistake ❌

You review the AI's pull request and find a problem.

You fix it, leave a comment, and merge.

The comment lived in a closed pull request, and the harness never heard about it.

You explained the same naming rule in three pull requests this week.

The fourth one is open right now.

You're the only memory your harness has.

And you're the most expensive part of it.

Problems Addressed 😔

  • Your most expensive reviewer spends their attention on findings a linter or a hook could catch.

  • Two reviewers carry two different rule sets in their heads, so they catch different things in the same code without standards.

  • The AI writes faster than you read, so reviewing every line becomes the bottleneck of the whole pipeline.

  • A big pull request buries the one decision that needed a human.

  • The harness stays frozen at the rules you guessed on day one, while the real mistakes of your codebase go unrecorded.

  • Design decisions made in a review stay undocumented, and the next reviewer has to rediscover them.

  • You can't tell whether your team improves, because nobody counts what reviews find.

  • Reviews that only fix the code never start the cycle Deming described, so the same finding keeps coming back.

How to Do It 🛠️

  1. Treat every human review comment as a defect in the harness, not only in the code.

  2. Sort the finding by who could have caught it: a linter or hook, a judge skill, a written decision, or only a human.

  3. Turn mechanical findings, like naming and formatting, into a hook or a lint rule.

  4. Turn semantic findings into a rule inside a validator skill that the AI reads fresh every session.

  5. Turn design findings into a written decision, and write down the reason next to it.

  6. Add the rejected code as a failing example in the pitfalls file.

  7. Start a rule suite in the harness, and write every human finding as a failing test case first: the rejected code is the input, and the test fails because nothing detects it yet.

  8. Write the rule that makes that test pass, then run the harness against the rejected diff with a criteria check, and keep the rule only if it blocks that diff.

  9. Ship the test and the rule in the same pull request as the fix, so the lesson merges together with the change.

  10. Send the next diffs through your pipeline first, so you only see what survives it.

  11. Tag every finding as nit, defect, design, or business rule, and count them per review.

  12. Run the contradiction audit every few weeks, since every new rule can disagree with an old one, and drop the hoarded rules the model has outgrown.

  13. Reserve your attention for the decisions the harness can't make: design trade-offs, business rules, and risk.

Benefits 🎯

  1. Protect your scarcest resource: You read what the harness can't judge, and nothing else.

  2. Never pay twice: A finding that became a rule is a finding you never write again.

  3. Grow from real pain: The harness collects the mistakes your codebase actually produces, instead of the ones you imagined on day one.

  4. Review the same way every time: Every diff meets the same rules, no matter which reviewer opens it.

  5. Merge faster: Fewer findings reach you, so the review of a small pull request ends sooner.

  6. Read your maturity: The mix of findings tells you how mature your team is, without a survey.

  7. Onboard people and agents: A new teammate or a new agent inherits every decision a human ever made, like a company brain.

Context 🧠

You generate code faster than anyone can read it, and you don't scale as a reviewer.

Mäntylä and Lassenius found that 60% to 75% of review defects were about evolvability: naming, structure, and documentation.

A comment in a pull request is a rule living in the wrong place.

The right place is the harness: a linter, a hook, a skill, or a written decision.

Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me.

Traditional proverb, first printed in 1651 by Anthony Weldon

Standards gates block the mechanical findings, so you climb toward design trade-offs and risk.

This is the loop in loop engineering: the evaluation checks every finding you move into it, no human needed.

The harness grows, and rules start to disagree, so you should audit your contradictions every few weeks.

Prompt Reference 📝

Bad Prompt 🚫 

Review this pull request.
Fix every problem you find.
Tell me when it's ready to merge.

Good prompt 👉 

You're reviewing this pull request as the harness, not as a person.

Read AGENTS.md, the standards, and the design decisions first.
Review the diff against them.
List every finding in a numbered table.

For each finding, say who should catch it next time.
Pick one: linter, hook, skill, or human.

Then propose the smallest harness change that catches it.
Write the rule, the file where it belongs, and a failing example.

Don't edit any code.
Don't edit any rule.
Ask me to approve each rule, one at a time.

Last, list the findings only a human should decide.
Explain why the harness can't.

A human reviewer found five issues with different severities.

Take the review comments on the pull request.
Write a failing test that represents each finding.
Watch it fail on the rejected code.
Write a rule that fixes the problem.
Add it to the code standards, style, architecture, and design suite.
That way, the finding never reaches a human reviewer again.

Considerations ⚠️

Not every finding deserves a rule.

A one-off judgment call about a strange edge case stays a comment.

A rule written after one comment can be wrong.

I wouldn't automate a rule after a single comment.

I'd wait for the second one.

You should test it on the rejected diff and on a clean one, so it blocks the first and lets the second pass.

Rules are code too, so they need review like any other change.

You don't leave the review.

You move to the decisions that matter, and that's a different job, not a smaller one.

I don't know yet how many findings per review a healthy team should see.

Zero would mean nobody is looking.

Type 📝

[X] Semi-Automatic

Limitations ⚠️

The first weeks cost more time, because you write the rule on top of the fix.

A judge skill costs tokens on every diff, so you should keep the cheap checks in linters.

A finding that depends on context nobody wrote down can't become a rule until you write that context.

articles.description: Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for...
articles.body_html:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

"What is the difference between a process and a thread?"

You have been asked this. You have probably asked it.

The standard answer goes: a process is heavy, a thread is light, and threads share memory.

That answer is true.

It is also the kind of true that you can recite for ten years without ever understanding what is going on underneath.

So let's skip the textbook and look at both from the seat where the decisions actually get made.

The kernel's seat.

Start with one long bar of RAM

Picture your machine's memory as a single long bar. Say 16 GB.

All of it belongs to the kernel. No program is allowed to touch it directly.

When you launch an app, the kernel creates a process to represent it, and carves out a slice of the bar as that process's private memory.

It writes down who owns which slice in a notebook, and it guards those boundaries.

Now watch it with real software.

You open a photo editor. The kernel makes a process for it, and the editor fills its slice with a 5 MB photo.

You also have Spotify open. That is a second process, with a second slice further down the bar.

The editor cannot read Spotify's memory. Spotify cannot read your photo.

If the editor reaches outside its slice, the kernel stops it on the spot.

And if Spotify crashes, your photo does not even flinch.

That wall is the entire reason one program cannot read or corrupt another's data.

A small confession about the bar

The bar is a teaching picture, and it is a little too tidy.

Real kernels do not hand out literal chunks of physical RAM. Every process gets its own virtual address space, and the CPU's memory management unit translates those addresses through page tables that the kernel controls.

Two processes can both use "address 0x1000" and land on completely different physical memory.

Touch an address that is not mapped for you, and the hardware raises a fault, and the kernel typically answers with a SIGSEGV.

The kernel's own memory docs cover the concepts if you want the full tour.

The wall in the picture is a very real wall. It is just made of page tables instead of drywall.

Now the editor wants to be fast

Brightening a photo one pixel at a time on a single core is slow.

So the editor asks the kernel for help: "give me four threads".

Here is the part that matters.

The kernel does not hand each thread more RAM.

It creates four lightweight tasks and points all of them at the same slice the process already owns.

Then it schedules those four tasks onto four cores, and they run at the same moment.

Each thread takes a quarter of the photo and brightens its own region, reading and writing the pixels directly where they sit.

Nothing was copied.

When the last thread finishes, the whole image is already brighter.

Now imagine doing the same job with four processes instead.

Each one needs its own slice. So the photo gets copied into all four, which is four times the memory.

Then somebody has to collect the four finished pieces and stitch them back together, which means sending data between processes with pipes, sockets or shared memory.

That is the entire pitch for threads in one sentence: they skip the copy, and they skip the stitching.

A fairness note for processes

I have been a bit mean to processes, so let me correct the record.

Modern fork() does not actually copy the whole photo up front. On Linux it is implemented with copy-on-write pages.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as parent
    participant K as kernel
    participant C as child

    P->>K: fork()
    K-->>C: new task, page tables copied, pages not copied
    Note over P,C: both see the same 5 MB, marked read-only
    C->>K: write to one pixel
    K->>K: page fault, copy just that one 4 KB page
    K-->>C: retry the write on the private copy
    Note over P,C: every untouched page is still shared

So the child starts almost for free, and only pays for pages it actually changes.

The picture above is the worst case, where every process rewrites everything. That is the case that happens when a job really does touch the whole photo.

The real difference is not "copy vs no copy" so much as "shared by default" vs "private by default".

And that, as we are about to see, is where all the trouble comes from.

The kernel's dirty secret: they are the same thing

Here is the sentence that rewired my head.

To the Linux kernel, a process and a thread are nearly the same object.

Both are just a task that the scheduler puts onto a CPU.

The scheduler does not schedule "processes". It schedules tasks. A four-thread process is four tasks that happen to be friends.

The only real difference is memory:

  • make a new task with a fresh slice, and you have a process
  • make a new task pointed at an existing slice, and you have a thread

On Linux that choice is one function: clone(), and one flag: CLONE_VM.

Do not take my word for it. Here is a tiny program that does the same write twice, once from a child process and once from a thread:

int brightness = 0;

void *worker(void *arg) { brightness = 100; return NULL; }

int main(void) {
    pid_t child = fork();
    if (child == 0) { brightness = 100; _exit(0); }   // a process writes
    waitpid(child, NULL, 0);
    printf("after a child PROCESS wrote 100: brightness = %d\n", brightness);

    pthread_t t;
    pthread_create(&t, NULL, worker, NULL);            // a thread writes
    pthread_join(t, NULL);
    printf("after a THREAD wrote 100:        brightness = %d\n", brightness);
}

I compiled it and ran it on Ubuntu 24.04:

after a child PROCESS wrote 100: brightness = 0
after a THREAD wrote 100:        brightness = 100

Same line of code in both. The process wrote into its own copy and the parent never saw it. The thread wrote into the copy.

Then I ran the same binary under strace -f -e trace=clone,clone3 to see what glibc really asked the kernel for (trimmed a little):

clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|CLONE_CHILD_SETTID|SIGCHLD)
clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|...})

The first line is fork(). No CLONE_VM.

The second is pthread_create(). There it is, CLONE_VM, plus friends.

Those friends decide what else gets shared:

  • CLONE_FILES: the open file descriptors
  • CLONE_SIGHAND: the signal handlers
  • CLONE_THREAD: the new task joins the same thread group, which is why getpid() returns the same number for every thread and the kernel hands each one its own thread id instead

(In my run the main thread and the worker both reported the same pid, and the worker had its own tid. The man page for gettid covers the details.)

And what is private to each thread? Its own stack, its own registers, and its own thread-local storage. Everything else, the heap and the globals and the open files, is shared.

A fun side effect of all this: containers are the same trick. Namespaces are created with CLONE_NEW* flags on the same clone() call. Linux has one very flexible "make a task" function, and the whole zoo of processes, threads and containers is just different flag combinations.

Danger one: two threads, one pixel

Now for the bill.

The kernel let all four threads into the same memory. That is the whole point. It is also the whole problem.

If two threads write the same pixel at the same time, you get a race condition.

Here is how it goes wrong. Both threads add 10 to a pixel that holds 50:

Both read 50. Both compute 60. Both write 60.

You expected 70. You got 60.

There is no crash. There is no error. One brighten operation simply evaporated.

I wanted a real number instead of a hand-wavy one, so I ran four threads, each bumping one shared counter a million times:

for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
    unsafe++;                      // shared, no protection
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
    safe++;                        // shared, behind a mutex
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
}

expected: 4000000
no lock:  3966879
mutex:    4000000

Over thirty thousand increments went missing, and the program exited happily. A second run lost a different amount.

That is what makes races miserable. They are not wrong in a consistent way. They are wrong in a different way every time, which is a spectacular property for a bug to have when you are trying to reproduce it.

The textbook fix is a lock. Only one thread at a time may touch the contended spot, and the rest wait their turn.

That works. It also costs you, because threads that wait are threads that are not working.

The better fix is to need no lock at all.

Look again at the photo example. Each thread was given its own quarter. Nobody writes anyone else's pixels, so nobody has to wait for anybody.

The best concurrency code is the kind where the threads rarely touch the same data. Partition first, lock only the seams.

Danger two: shared memory means shared fate

The second bill is nastier because it is not subtle.

All four threads live in one address space. So when one of them does something the kernel considers fatal, the kernel has no way of killing "just that thread".

A segmentation fault on any thread, and the default action for that signal is to terminate the whole process.

I did not want to just claim that, so I tried it. One thread ticks along. Another sleeps half a second, then writes through a null pointer:

steady thread: tick 1
steady thread: tick 2
steady thread: tick 3
Segmentation fault (core dumped)       # exit code 139

The steady thread had two more ticks to go. It never got them.

Three perfectly healthy threads, executed for the crime of sharing an address space with a guilty one.

The same logic applies to quieter failures. A buffer overflow in one thread can scribble over memory that another thread is using, and the crash shows up somewhere completely unrelated, an hour later.

Meanwhile Spotify, a separate process, is still playing. That wall from the first picture just paid for itself.

So which one do I pick?

You can see this trade-off baked into real software.

Chrome gives each site its own process, so one rogue tab cannot take the browser down with it. Isolation is worth the memory.

PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, so a crashing backend does not take the whole database with it. Isolation is worth the memory there too.

On the other side, anything that crunches one big shared dataset on many cores, like our photo brightener, wants threads, because copying and stitching would eat the speedup.

(And if you are in Python, the GIL means threads will not run your Python bytecode in parallel in the standard build, which is why so many people reach for processes there. That is a language story, not a kernel one.)

Here is the decision as a flowchart:

flowchart TD
    A[you need concurrency] --> B{must one failure<br/>stay contained?}
    B -->|yes: untrusted code,<br/>plugins, separate tenants| P[processes]
    B -->|no| C{do the workers need to<br/>share lots of data fast?}
    C -->|no| P2[processes,<br/>simpler and safer]
    C -->|yes| D{can you partition the data so<br/>threads rarely touch the same bytes?}
    D -->|yes| T[threads,<br/>almost no locks]
    D -->|no| T2[threads plus locks,<br/>and budget for the debugging]

    classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef proc fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef thr fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

    class B,C,D decision
    class A start
    class P,P2 proc
    class T,T2 thr

The 30 second interview answer

If somebody asks you the question tomorrow, here is the whole thing:

  1. The kernel gives every process its own private memory, and the wall between processes is why one app cannot corrupt another.
  2. A thread is a task the kernel points at memory that already exists, so threads share one address space and nothing gets copied.
  3. On Linux both are made by clone(). The difference is basically one flag, CLONE_VM.
  4. Sharing is the speed, and it is also the two dangers: races when threads touch the same data, and shared fate when one thread crashes.

"Threads are lightweight" was never wrong.

It just left out what you are paying with.


Your team's attention is limited, and the deluge of AI-generated code is making it harder to keep production secure and reliable without slowing you down.

Instead of presenting every diff with equal emphasis, LiveReview scores each change by blast radius — how far its impact reaches through your call graph — so you can focus attention where it actually matters.
