articles.title: TypeScript Is Unsound on Purpose: 7 Programs That Type-Check, Then Crash
articles.description: TypeScript's design goals rule out a sound type system. Here are 7 programs that pass tsc --strict, throw at runtime, and the fix for each.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Non-goal number three on the TypeScript Design Goals page reads: "Apply a sound or 'provably correct' type system. Instead, strike a balance between correctness and productivity." The team wrote that down on purpose.

The handbook says the same thing in its own words. The type compatibility chapter has a section called "A Note on Soundness" that says TypeScript "allows certain operations that can't be known at compile-time to be safe," and that the places where it does so "were carefully considered."

So a green tsc --strict run tells you your code stayed inside the trade-offs the team picked, and those trade-offs include programs that throw a TypeError. Below are seven programs that compile under --strict and fail at runtime, the rule that lets each one through, and what closes it, where something does. Every rule is linked to the doc that states it, so you can paste any snippet into the TypeScript playground and check it yourself.

What --strict covers, and what it skips

The strict flag turns on the strict family: strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, noImplicitAny, useUnknownInCatchVariables and five more. Two checks that matter below are not in that family: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes. The TypeScript 4.1 release notes say the index check "is not automatically enabled by the strict flag" because "it might be noisy for a lot of code."

Every snippet here assumes --strict and nothing else. One of them dies the moment you add a single line to tsconfig.json. The rest need a pattern, a lint rule, or a runtime check, because no flag exists for them.

Variance: the array and the method

1. A cat in the dog array 

class Animal {
  name = "animal";
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  bark() { return "woof"; }
}
class Cat extends Animal {
  meow() { return "meow"; }
}

function adoptCat(shelter: Animal[]) {
  shelter.push(new Cat());
}

const kennel: Dog[] = [new Dog()];
adoptCat(kennel);
for (const dog of kennel) dog.bark(); // TypeError on the Cat

Dog[] is assignable to Animal[] because arrays relate covariantly: if Dog fits Animal, then Dog[] fits Animal[]. That is safe for reading and wrong for writing. push takes an Animal, the Cat goes in, and the loop calls bark on a cat.

The fix: when a function only reads, type the parameter as readonly Animal[]. push doesn't exist on that type, so the write becomes a compile error. Callers can still pass a Dog[], because the handbook notes that a mutable array assigns to a ReadonlyArray but not the other way around.

2. The method that only takes strings 

interface Handler {
  handle(input: string | number): void;
}

const h: Handler = {
  handle(input: string) {
    console.log(input.toUpperCase());
  },
};

h.handle(42); // TypeError at runtime: no toUpperCase on 42

strictFunctionTypes arrived in TypeScript 2.6 and checks function parameters contravariantly. It skips methods on purpose. The release notes say the stricter check covers all function types "except those originating in method or constructor declarations," and that "methods are excluded specifically to ensure generic classes and interfaces (such as Array<T>) continue to mostly relate covariantly." The TSConfig reference adds that the team found "a large number of inherently unsafe class hierarchies, including some in the DOM" while building the flag.

So a member written in method syntax stays bivariant, and an implementation that only accepts string gets through. That same carve-out is why program 1 compiles: push is a method on Array<T>.

The fix: declare the member as a property, handle: (input: string | number) => void. Now the same object literal is a compile error. The typescript-eslint rule method-signature-style enforces property style by default, and its docs state that "methods are always bivariant in their arguments, while function properties are contravariant."

Promises the checker doesn't track

3. A narrowed field that changes under you 

interface Profile {
  readonly nickname: string | null;
}

function greet(p: Profile, onGreet: () => void) {
  if (p.nickname !== null) {
    onGreet();
    console.log(p.nickname.toUpperCase());
  }
}

const live = { nickname: "kit" as string | null };
greet(live, () => {
  live.nickname = null;
}); // TypeError at runtime: nickname is null

The object types handbook page says TypeScript "doesn't factor in whether properties on two types are readonly when checking whether those types are compatible, so readonly properties can also change via aliasing." live is mutable, greet sees it through a readonly lens, and the callback writes through the original reference. Delete readonly from Profile and the program still compiles. The modifier was never the guard.

What actually lets it through is narrowing. After p.nickname !== null, the compiler keeps that narrowing across the onGreet() call. Issue #9998, "Trade-offs in Control Flow Analysis", explains why: resetting every narrowing after every call is the pessimistic option, and Anders Hejlsberg called the optimistic assumption "the best compromise."

No flag covers this one. Copy the value into a local before you call out, const nick = p.nickname;, then check and use nick. A callback can't reassign your const, so that narrowing holds. And keep the asymmetry in mind: readonly arrays are checked, readonly properties are not.

4. The key that isn't there 

const ports: Record<string, number> = { web: 8080 };

const db = ports["db"]; // typed as number
console.log(db.toFixed(0)); // TypeError at runtime: db is undefined

An index signature like Record<string, number> promises a number for any string key. ports["db"] is typed number and holds undefined. Arrays behave the same way: reading past the end gives you the element type, not undefined.

The fix: noUncheckedIndexedAccess. It adds undefined to every read through an index signature and every array index, so db.toFixed stops compiling until you check it. The cost is noise in index-based for loops, and the 4.1 notes point you at for...of or forEach instead.

Information lost on the way up

5. The optional property that was there all along 

interface Base {
  id: string;
}
interface Job {
  id: string;
  retries?: number;
}

const raw = { id: "job-1", retries: "three" };
const base: Base = raw; // extra property: fine
const job: Job = base; // missing optional: fine

console.log(job.retries?.toFixed(0)); // TypeError at runtime

Two legal steps. raw to Base: excess property checks run only on a fresh object literal, and the handbook's excess property checks section says assigning the object to another variable gets around them. Base to Job: Base has no retries, and a missing property satisfies an optional one. In the middle, the compiler forgets retries existed. At the end it assumes number | undefined. The string "three" isn't nullish, so ?. doesn't save you.

Nothing in tsconfig closes this. exactOptionalPropertyTypes only controls whether you may write undefined into an optional property. Exact object types, which would close it, have been an open proposal in issue #12936 since December 2016. When a reader raised this case on his Effective TypeScript repo, Dan Vanderkam called it "definitely another source of unsoundness" and pointed to Item 48 of his book, which covers it. The pattern that works: don't round-trip objects through a narrower interface, and validate data at the boundary where it enters your program.

Where you told the compiler to trust you

6. The assertion that skipped the check 

interface Account {
  id: string;
  roles: string[];
}

const body = '{"id":"u1"}';
const data: unknown = JSON.parse(body);
const account = data as Account;

console.log(account.roles.includes("admin")); // TypeError

The everyday types handbook page says type assertions "are removed by the compiler," and that "there won't be an exception or null generated if the type assertion is wrong." The cast from unknown is allowed because assertions may move to a "more specific or less specific version of a type." account.roles is undefined at runtime.

The fix: replace the cast with a runtime check, either a schema validator such as Zod or a hand-written guard (see program 7 before you trust one). To ban casts outright, typescript-eslint's consistent-type-assertions accepts assertionStyle: "never", which still allows as const.

7. The type guard that lies 

type Cat = { kind: "cat"; meow(): string };
type Dog = { kind: "dog"; bark(): string };

function isCat(pet: Cat | Dog): pet is Cat {
  return "bark" in pet; // inverted check, still compiles
}

function adopt(): Cat | Dog {
  return { kind: "dog", bark: () => "woof" };
}

const pet = adopt();
if (isCat(pet)) {
  pet.meow(); // TypeError at runtime: a Dog has no meow
}

A type predicate is a promise you make. The compiler doesn't prove it. The narrowing handbook page says that whenever a guard is called, TypeScript "will narrow that variable to that specific type if the original type is compatible." It reads the signature. Nothing compares the body with the claim. Dan Vanderkam's post on unsoundness makes the same point: with a guard, "you're still asserting that your type guard really guards the type."

The fix: since TypeScript 5.5, the compiler can infer a predicate from the body when four conditions hold: no explicit return type or predicate annotation, a single return, no mutation of the parameter, and a boolean expression tied to a refinement of the parameter. An inferred predicate comes from the check itself, so the two can't disagree. Keep explicit predicates for checks the compiler can't follow, and give each one a unit test with a matching and a non-matching value.

Does TypeScript 7 change any of this?

TypeScript 7.0 shipped on July 8, 2026, with the compiler ported to Go in the typescript-go repo. The announcement says the port kept "the structure and logic of the original codebase" to keep results consistent, and that 7.0 "is made to be compatible with TypeScript 6.0's type-checking and command-line behavior."

The differences it lists are elsewhere: flags deprecated in 6.0 become hard errors, strict now defaults to true, template literal types preserve Unicode code points, JSDoc support was reworked, and changing the --checkers count can surface order-dependent results. None of those touch the seven rules above, so by the team's own compatibility statement all seven still compile on 7.0. The new strict default doesn't help either, since every program here already passes --strict.

The seven, side by side:

# Hole What closes it
1 Array covariance readonly T[] parameters
2 Method bivariance Property-style members, method-signature-style
3 Narrowing kept across a callback Copy to a const before callbacks
4 Unchecked index reads noUncheckedIndexedAccess
5 Optional-property widening Validate at the boundary (no flag)
6 Assertions Runtime validation, assertionStyle: "never"
7 Lying type guards Inferred predicates, tested guards

And the one config line that costs nothing to add:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true
  }
}

TypeScript gives you a checker that catches most mistakes and tells you in writing which ones it lets through. Add noUncheckedIndexedAccess today, and put the other six on your review checklist.

If this was useful

Every program in this post comes down to one question: what does assignability actually check? The TypeScript Type System is the book on that question. It covers variance and bivariance, including the function-versus-method split behind programs 1 and 2, plus the generic, conditional and branded types you reach for when the built-in rules are too loose.

The TypeScript Library has five books. Start with the first two if TypeScript is your main language, swap in a bridge book if you are coming from the JVM or PHP, and add the fifth if you ship TypeScript at work:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Why Google Analytics breaks inside a Figma plugin, and what I built instead
articles.description: I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community...
articles.body_html:
I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community page. Neither one says whether anybody opened the plugin this week, or which of its buttons they pressed.

The usual answer on the web is Google Analytics. Paste the gtag snippet into a plugin's ui.html, open the console, and you get this:

SecurityError: Failed to read the 'cookie' property from 'Document':
Cookies are disabled inside 'data:' URLs.

The snippet is fine. The place it runs in is the problem, and that place turned out to be interesting enough that I ended up writing my own SDK for it. This post is about what I ran into.

A plugin is two programs

The first program is the main code, usually code.ts. It runs in a sandbox next to the document. It has the figma API and fetch. It has no DOM, no window and no document.

The second program is the UI. You pass an HTML string to figma.showUI(), and Figma loads that string into an iframe. The page gets a data: URL, so its origin is null.

Cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB all belong to an origin. A null origin owns none of them, and reading any of them throws. That is the error above.

The two programs cannot call each other. They talk through postMessage, and that is the only channel.

So the half that knows who the user is (the sandbox, through figma.currentUser) cannot see a click. The half that sees every click (the iframe) cannot remember anything and does not know who is clicking.

Web analytics assumes one page with a cookie jar. I had two halves and no jar.

Problem 1: the key is on one side, the buttons on the other

I wanted the developer to write the API key once. The sandbox is the right place for it, because the Figma data is there too:

// code.ts
import { tode } from '@tode-sdk/core';

figma.showUI(__html__);
await tode.init({ apiKey: 'your-api-key' });

init() reads the user id, the plugin id, the editor type (Figma, FigJam, Dev Mode, Slides) and posts all of it to the iframe in one message:

figma.ui.postMessage({ type: 'TODE_DATA', message: config });

The UI adapter listens for that message and configures itself. After that, both halves can send events with the same identity.

That is the happy path. It has a hole in it.

Problem 2: the first message gets lost

figma.showUI() returns before the iframe has loaded anything. If init() is fast and the UI bundle is slow, the config is posted to a page with no listener yet. Nobody hears it, the UI never becomes ready, and no error appears anywhere.

The same thing happens when a plugin closes its UI and calls showUI() again later. The new iframe starts empty.

The fix is a handshake that starts from the UI. When an adapter attaches its listener, it asks:

window.parent.postMessage(
  { pluginMessage: { type: 'TODE_UI_READY' }, pluginId: '*' },
  '*',
);

The sandbox answers by posting the config again. One detail matters here. Most plugins already set figma.ui.onmessage for their own messages, and assigning it a second time would overwrite their handler. figma.ui.on('message', ...) adds a listener next to it and leaves theirs alone, so the SDK uses that.

The plugin's own handler still receives the TODE_UI_READY message. It has to ignore message types it does not know, which a well-written handler does anyway.

Problem 3: events that fire before the SDK is ready

A common first event is "plugin opened". It fires on mount, before the config has crossed over from the sandbox.

My first version told developers to wrap every call in if (isReady). That is a rule people forget, and the event they lose is the most important one.

Now the SDK keeps early events in a queue with the time they happened, and sends them when the config arrives:

if (this._isReady && this._apiKey) {
  await this.send(event);
  return;
}
if (this._queue.length >= MAX_QUEUED_EVENTS) return; // 50
this._queue.push(event); // event.timestamp was set at call time

The cap is 50. If something calls trackAction in a loop while the SDK is not ready, I would rather drop events than grow an array forever inside someone else's plugin.

Problem 4: how long is a session

On a website, session length comes from page views with timestamps and a timeout. A plugin has no pages. It has a panel that is open for a while and then is gone.

I did not want to depend on an unload event firing in an iframe that Figma can remove at any moment. So I turned the question around. The UI opens a WebSocket when it becomes ready and holds it. The server writes down when the socket opened. When the socket closes, for any reason, the server writes one session row with the duration.

A closed panel, a closed tab and a crashed browser all look the same to the server: the socket is gone. No goodbye message is needed.

The client sends ping every 5 seconds. If the server hears nothing for 60 seconds, it ends the session itself, so a dead connection cannot inflate the numbers.

That covers a panel someone opens and closes. Three other cases needed more work.

The first is laptop sleep. People leave a plugin open, close the lid and come back hours later. The socket is dead and the panel is still on screen. The SDK reconnects with backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, capped at 30s) and never gives up while the UI is open. It also listens for the browser's online event and retries at once when the network is back.

The second follows from the first. Each reconnect is a new session row on the server. Every connection carries the same session_id, generated once per UI load, so the rows can be grouped later.

The third is React. Five components calling useTode() used to mean five sockets and five sessions for one person. The socket is now shared and reference-counted. The first caller opens it, and it closes when the last holder is gone.

Problem 5: analytics must never break the plugin

If my server is down, a designer's export button still has to work. So nothing in the SDK throws. init() and trackAction() catch everything and log to the console.

The sandbox made this harder than I expected. It has fetch, and it has no AbortController. Its fetch ignores signal. A request that hangs cannot be cancelled there, which means await tode.init() could block a plugin's startup.

The workaround is a race against a timer:

if (typeof AbortController === 'undefined') {
  const timeout = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timed out')), 10_000);
  });
  return Promise.race([fetch(url, rest), timeout])
    .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

The request itself may still be hanging somewhere. The plugin has stopped waiting for it, and that is the part I care about.

Counting people without a cookie

A cookie exists on the web because the page does not know who you are. A plugin does. figma.currentUser.id is stable for a Figma account, and you get it by adding one line to the manifest:

{
  "permissions": ["currentuser"],
  "networkAccess": {
    "allowedDomains": [
      "https://processing.usetode.dev",
      "wss://processing.usetode.dev"
    ]
  }
}

That id is enough to tell a new user from a returning one, which is where retention comes from. The SDK sends the id and nothing else about the person: no name, no email, no file contents.

Country is looked up on the server from the request IP. The IP is not stored.

Without the currentuser permission, figma.currentUser is null. The SDK sends an empty value in that case and events still arrive. You lose unique users and keep everything else.

What it looks like from the plugin side

After all of that, the part a plugin developer writes is small:

import { useTode } from '@tode-sdk/figma-react';

function ExportButton() {
  const { trackAction, trackActionWithMetric } = useTode();

  const onExport = async () => {
    const layers = await exportSelection();
    trackAction('export_clicked');
    trackActionWithMetric('layers_exported', layers.length);
  };

  return <button onClick={onExport}>Export</button>;
}

There are adapters for React, Vue, Angular, Svelte and plain TypeScript. They are thin. The queue, the handshake and the socket all live in the core package, so I only fix each bug once.

What I have not solved

There is no way to learn from plugin code that an event failed to deliver. Failures go to console.error and that is all. I chose silence over callbacks because I did not want analytics error handling in people's plugins, and I am still not sure it was the right call.

Sessions need a UI. A plugin that runs a command with no panel has no iframe to hold a socket, so it gets events and no session length.

And a reconnect still shows up as a separate row on the server. The shared session_id makes it fixable, and I have not built the merge yet.

If you want to look at the code

The SDK is MIT licensed and lives at github.com/kolebayev/tode-sdk. The service behind it is tode. It has a free plan for one plugin, and the paid plans are how I cover the servers.

If you came here for the Google Analytics error and want the long answer, I wrote up what the Measurement Protocol can and cannot do inside a plugin.

I would like to hear from people who build extensions for other hosts, like VS Code, Chrome or Sketch. How do you find out whether anyone uses what you shipped?

articles.title: I Built a Life Simulator That Deals You a Random Country at Birth — With Real UN Data
articles.description: Every life simulator starts the same way: you design your character. Pick a country, pick a family,...
articles.body_html:
Every life simulator starts the same way: you design your character. Pick a country, pick a family, optimize the stats. I wanted the opposite. Real life doesn't let you pick — you are dealt a country, a family, a body, at random, weighted by how many babies are actually born in each place. So I built a game around the deal itself: 1in8b.dev — "1 in 8 billion". You press one button, and you are born somewhere on Earth, with probabilities proportional to real birth counts. Then you live that life, year by year, until the local statistics say you don't.

The data layer

The whole game runs on public statistics for 172 countries and territories:

  • UN World Population Prospects for life tables and birth counts
  • WHO / World Bank indicators for life expectancy, under-5 mortality, income (GDP per capita, PPP), urbanization, fertility
  • Cause-of-death distributions per country — what people actually die of in Lagos is not what they die of in Osaka

That last one matters more than I expected. In the dataset, life expectancy runs from 54.5 years (Nigeria) to 85.5 (Hong Kong) — a 31-year gap determined almost entirely by the flag next to your birthplace. A simulation that ignores that is just a dice game. A simulation that uses it becomes something else: every run is a small lesson in how much of a "life outcome" is dealt before any choice is made. Mechanically, each in-game year rolls against the country's survival curve, its cause-of-death profile, and milestone events (schooling, work, migration, family) whose probabilities shift with the country's stats. Rich-country lives and poor-country lives don't just end at different ages — they have different shapes.

The build

It's a static site — vanilla JS, no framework, no backend, no accounts. All data ships as JSON and the simulation runs entirely in the browser. Two details from the build that might be useful to others:

1. Nine languages as static routes, not runtime switching. Each language is its own pre-built page (/ja/, /ko/, /fr/ …) with its own title, description, and canonical URL. The app detects the language from the path. This cost some duplication and bought a lot: every language version is independently indexable, and the first paint is already in the right language.

2. Country names are a real i18n problem. A UI string table is the easy part. But the game also needs the names of all 172 countries in every language — plus region names. We had Chinese, English, and Korean in the data; the other six languages were showing Chinese country names to French and Thai players. The fix was CLDR data (via Intl.DisplayNames) for the missing names, wired through one countryName() helper — and auditing ~250 hardcoded bilingual strings that had quietly bypassed the string table entirely. If your app "supports 9 languages," the long tail of strings outside the table is where it actually doesn't.

Try it

It's free, no sign-up, runs in the browser: 1in8b.dev

Play one life as yourself-by-birthplace, then re-roll and see who else you could have been. The second run is usually the one that sticks with you.

articles.title: Verify CBE and Telebirr payments in your app with a free API
articles.description: Customers in Ethiopia pay by bank transfer and send a screenshot. Here's how to confirm the payment against the bank's own record from Node or Python: one REST call, no API key, and a self-hosted option for Telebirr.
articles.body_html:
If you sell anything online in Ethiopia, you know the flow: the customer pays by bank transfer or Telebirr, then sends a screenshot. Someone on your team looks at it and decides whether to ship. Screenshots are easy to edit and easy to reuse, so that decision is a guess.

I maintain cheki.et, a free, MIT-licensed receipt checker, and this post is the developer version: how to confirm a payment against the bank's own record from your backend, in a few lines of Node or Python.

One thing first, because it's the most common confusion I see. Searching "telebirr api" or "cbe api" mostly turns up payment collection: merchant APIs where you start a payment and get a callback. Those need a merchant agreement with the bank. What I'm describing is the other half. The customer has already paid, the normal way, and you want to check the receipt they sent you. That needs no contract with anyone, because Ethiopian banks and wallets publish every receipt at a public URL.

How it works

Each bank has its own receipt page: transactioninfo.ethiotelecom.et/receipt/{number} for Telebirr, mbreciept.cbe.com.et/{receiptId} for CBE, a JSON endpoint for Bank of Abyssinia, a PDF for CBE Birr, and so on. cheki fetches the right one, parses it, runs a few sanity checks (positive amount, the reference you asked for, no failed or pending status), and returns the same JSON for every bank. There are 10 banks and wallets live: CBE, Telebirr, BOA, M-Pesa, Dashen, Awash, CBE Birr, Siinqee, eBirr and ZamZam. Three of those (M-Pesa, ZamZam, CBE Birr) are marked beta because they've been checked against few or no real receipts.

One request 

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"}'

No signup and no API key. The body takes bank plus whatever that bank needs:

Field When
reference Almost always: a receipt link, Receipt ID, transaction number or FT Ref
accountNumber BOA (last 5 digits) and older CBE FT receipts (last 8 digits)
phoneNumber CBE Birr (the payer's phone)
qrData A scanned QR payload (BOA, CBE Birr, Telebirr)

That reference is made up, so you'll get a 422 back. A confirmed receipt looks like this (names and numbers are fake):

{
  "success": true,
  "verified": true,
  "bank": "Commercial Bank of Ethiopia",
  "bankCode": "cbe",
  "reference": "FT26SAMPLE01",
  "senderName": "ABEBE KEBEDE",
  "receiverName": "TIGIST ALEMU",
  "receiverAccount": "1****6171",
  "amount": 1250.5,
  "currency": "ETB",
  "date": "2026-10-01",
  "sourceUrl": "https://apps.cbe.com.et:100/?id=FT26SAMPLE0100006171",
  "cached": false
}

The rule that matters: only verified: true means the bank confirmed it. success: true only means the request was handled. A BOA QR that BOA couldn't confirm comes back with success: true, verified: false, decodedOnly: true, and a QR can be copied. Don't ship on that.

The error codes are what you'd expect: 400 bad input, 404 unknown bank, 413 body too large, 422 the bank has no such receipt, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After), 502 the bank couldn't be reached. A 502 for a geo-blocked bank includes a fallbackUrl, which is the bank's own receipt page.

Node: cheki-verify 

npm install cheki-verify   # 1.6.0, no dependencies, Node 20+

Here's the check I'd run before marking an order paid. Confirm it with the bank, then make sure it's actually this order's payment:

import { Cheki, isVerified, ChekiAPIError } from "cheki-verify";

const cheki = new Cheki();
const seen = new Set(); // use a UNIQUE column in your database instead

async function checkPayment(order, bank, reference) {
  let r;
  try {
    r = await cheki.verify(bank, reference);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof ChekiAPIError) {
      // 422: the bank has no such receipt. 502 + fallbackUrl: bank not reachable from the server.
      return { ok: false, why: e.serverMessage ?? e.message, openAtBank: e.fallbackUrl };
    }
    throw e; // network error or timeout: try again later, don't accept
  }
  if (!isVerified(r)) return { ok: false, why: "not confirmed by the bank" };
  if (r.amount !== order.amount) return { ok: false, why: `amount is ${r.amount}` };
  if (!r.receiverAccount?.endsWith(order.accountLast4)) return { ok: false, why: "paid to another account" };
  const key = `${r.bankCode}:${r.reference}`;
  if (seen.has(key)) return { ok: false, why: "receipt already used" };
  seen.add(key);
  return { ok: true, payer: r.senderName, date: r.date };
}

console.log(await checkPayment({ amount: 1250.5, accountLast4: "6171" }, "dashen", "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"));

The last two checks are the ones people skip. A real receipt for a transfer to someone else's account passes isVerified. So does a real receipt the same customer already used last week. The bank can't know about your orders, so those checks have to live in your code.

In the TypeScript SDK, any non-2xx response throws a ChekiAPIError (with statusCode, fallbackUrl and checkedUrl), and a 429 throws ChekiRateLimitError. It retries at most once, and only where that's safe.

Python: cheki 

pip install cheki   # 1.6.0, needs only requests, Python 3.10+

The Python client returns a result for API errors instead of raising, so it reads as one if:

from cheki import ChekiClient

with ChekiClient() as cheki:
    r = cheki.verify("cbe", "https://mbreciept.cbe.com.et/fHCxExampleRcpt01")

    if r.is_verified:
        print(r.sender_name, "paid", r.amount, r.currency, "to", r.receiver_account, "on", r.date)
    elif r.fallback_url:
        print("Bank not reachable from the server. Open:", r.fallback_url)
    else:
        print(f"Not verified ({r.http_status}): {r.error}")

It also installs a small CLI, which is handy in a terminal: cheki-verify telebirr DET0SAMPLE --json. It exits 0 only when the bank confirmed the receipt.

End-of-day reconciliation

POST /api/verify/batch takes up to 20 receipts:

curl -X POST https://cheki.et/api/verify/batch \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"receipts": [
        {"bank": "dashen", "reference": "B22WDTI00SAMPLE1"},
        {"bank": "boa", "reference": "FT26SAMPLE07", "accountNumber": "12345"}
      ]}'

You get back total, verified, failed, cached and one result per receipt. Both SDKs wrap it as verifyBatch / verify_batch.

Limits and what's kept

  • Server side only. The API sends no CORS headers, so call it from your backend, not the browser.
  • Rate limits per IP: 30 checks a minute (each batch item counts), and 5 batch requests a minute. The SDKs export RECOMMENDED_BATCH_CHUNK (15) for long lists.
  • Storage: no accounts and no database. A receipt the bank confirmed stays in the server's memory for up to six hours, so a repeat check returns cached: true without asking the bank again. Failed checks are never kept.

The full reference is in the API docs, and the developer page has the Go, PHP and Dart SDKs as well.

Telebirr and M-Pesa: self-host it

Telebirr's and M-Pesa's receipt pages only answer requests from Ethiopian networks. The hosted cheki.et API runs in Frankfurt, so for those two it returns a 502 with fallbackUrl. That's fine for a person at a counter, who can open the link on their phone, but not for an automated checkout.

The fix is to run your own copy on a server in Ethiopia:

git clone https://github.com/1RB/cheki.git
cd cheki
docker compose up -d   # serves on http://localhost:3000

Then point the SDK at it:

const cheki = new Cheki({ baseUrl: "http://your-server:3000" });

cheki = ChekiClient(base_url="http://your-server:3000")

Every option is an environment variable, and all are optional. For example, CHEKI_CACHE=off turns off the in-memory cache if you'd rather keep nothing. There's a longer walkthrough in the self-hosting guide.

Other options

cheki isn't the only way to do this. check.et, verify.et and qbirr offer hosted APIs with keys and dashboards, and there are open-source libraries if you'd rather parse receipts inside your own app, such as tx-verify for Python and telebirr-receipt for Node. They all read the same public receipt pages. Pick based on which banks you need, whether you want an account and a dashboard, and whether you can run something on an Ethiopian network.

Help wanted

The weakest spots are the beta banks. If you have a real M-Pesa, ZamZam or CBE Birr receipt that cheki gets wrong, an issue on GitHub with the names and accounts redacted helps a lot. The repo has npm run probe -- <receipt-url> --redact for exactly that.

cheki.et is MIT licensed and isn't affiliated with any bank or Ethio Telecom.

Ray (@1RB on GitHub)

articles.title: DORA for Financial-Sector Suppliers: Essential Preparations for ICT Providers
articles.description: Understand the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and prep your ICT services for compliance in the financial sector.
articles.body_html:
Introduction

The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is a significant legislative measure aimed at ensuring that the financial sector is resilient against IT disruptions. As a financial-sector supplier, particularly those providing Information and Communication Technology (ICT) services, understanding DORA's implications and preparing accordingly is crucial. This article outlines necessary actions for ICT providers under DORA to ensure compliance and foster resilience in their services.

What is DORA?

DORA aims to strengthen the IT resilience of the European financial space. It is designed to address challenges posed by increasing digitalization in the sector, ensuring a comprehensive approach to operational resilience. Its requirements cover various aspects, including risk management, testing, and reporting, effectively shaping the regulatory landscape in which ICT suppliers operate.

Understanding DORA’s Core Requirements

DORA introduces several key regulations that ICT providers must adhere to:

1. Risk Management Frameworks

Providers need to develop comprehensive risk management frameworks that identify, assess, and manage ICT risks effectively. This involves:

  • Conducting regular risk assessments.
  • Establishing governance structures that include accountability for digital resilience.
  • Defining risk appetite and tolerance levels.

2. Incident Reporting

ICT providers must implement effective incident detection and reporting mechanisms. The requirements include:

  • The establishment of protocols for detection, management, and reporting of ICT-related incidents.
  • Timely notification of incidents to relevant authorities and stakeholders, ideally within 24 hours.

3. Testing and Validation of Resilience

DORA mandates that ICT suppliers perform regular testing of their operational resilience. Recommended practices include:

  • Conducting stress tests and scenario analyses to assess the robustness of systems.
  • Implementing a framework for coordination with financial institutions during testing phases to ensure alignment and understanding.

4. Third-party Risk Management

ICT suppliers must also have strategies in place to manage third-party risks. This involves:

  • Due diligence assessments of vendors to evaluate their operational resilience.
  • Continuous monitoring of third-party risks throughout the relationship.

Steps to Prepare for DORA Compliance

Preparing for DORA compliance entails several action steps that ICT providers must undertake:

1. Conduct a Gap Assessment

Start with a comprehensive gap assessment to understand your current standing in relation to DORA requirements. Identify areas where your processes and controls may fall short. This assessment should ideally include:

  • A review of existing policies and procedures.
  • Identification of compliance gaps, including both technical and procedural weaknesses.

2. Enhance Your Risk Management Framework

Based on findings from the gap assessment, enhance your risk management framework to meet DORA’s expectations. Focus on:

  • Integrating IT risk management with overall business risk management.
  • Documenting processes clearly and establishing accountability for risk management tasks.

3. Develop Incident Management Protocols

Establish incident management protocols that align with DORA’s requirements. Ensure that your protocols include:

  • Clear definitions of what constitutes an incident.
  • Procedures for timely communication and escalation within the organization.

4. Implement Continuous Monitoring Practices

DORA requires that ICT providers have mechanisms in place for continuous monitoring of their ICT systems. This may include:

  • Deployment of automated monitoring tools to detect anomalies.
  • Regular audits and reviews to assess the effectiveness of existing controls and processes.

Cross-Framework Mapping

Understanding how DORA aligns with other regulatory frameworks is essential for ICT suppliers working in multiple jurisdictions. Cross-framework mapping can help:

  • Identify overlapping requirements between DORA, ISO 27001, SOC 2, and other standards, enabling organizations to streamline their compliance efforts.
  • Reduce redundancy and overlap in efforts to establish a cohesive compliance strategy.

Security Testing for Compliance

Regular security testing is vital for demonstrating compliance with DORA. Consider the following:

  • Engage in penetration testing programs to simulate real-world attacks and evaluate system vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly conduct vulnerability assessments to identify and remediate security weaknesses in a timely manner.

Evidence and Audit Preparation

Preparing for potential audits requires documenting compliance efforts thoroughly. Key activities include:

  • Collecting evidence that demonstrates adherence to DORA requirements.
  • Maintaining an organized record of policies, risk assessments, incident reports, and security testing outcomes.

The Role of Bitkosh Technologies

While this article has focused on the necessary preparations for ICT providers under DORA, organizations may benefit from professional guidance. Bitkosh Technologies specializes in compliance readiness and can assist in gap assessments, cross-framework mappings, and evidence preparation. Such support can enhance your operational processes and increase the likelihood of a successful audit.

Conclusion

As the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) comes into effect, ICT providers serving the financial sector must take proactive steps to prepare. Understanding its core requirements and implementing the necessary framework adjustments are crucial for compliance and operational resilience. By engaging in proactive risk management, effective incident response planning, and targeted security testing, ICT providers can not only comply with DORA but also contribute to a more resilient financial ecosystem.
